Following Donald Trump’s election as President of the United States, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. After the new US administration takes office, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two respects—from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation—with potentially far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, the risks facing emerging market economies have increased amid a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar and the possibility that the United States may adopt trade protectionist measures. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained favourable, and overall loan growth increased further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes and, more broadly, US policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and the potential impact on local interest rates. Following Donald Trump’s election as President of the United States, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only did the election result surprise the market, but the associated market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that measures introduced by Trump, such as tax reform, increased infrastructure spending and deregulation, would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. After the new US administration takes office, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two respects—from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation—which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. However, the Trump tax cuts anticipated by the market may not provide the expected stimulus to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity already close to its potential, fiscal stimulus measures may provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth, while increasing upside risks to US inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will therefore significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening, long-term bond yields have already risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, rising trade protectionism would create a “lose-lose” outcome for both the United States and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that undermine overall welfare, impede global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the still-fragile European economic recovery. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows arising from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation has increased. This could weigh on economic growth and heighten the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations that the Trump administration will pursue large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns over a sharp rise in energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, resulting in broad-based and significant increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings indicate that, since the 2013 “taper tantrum”, the influence of the US Treasury market on sovereign bond markets has intensified, and that US interest rate hikes and tighter financial conditions would have a significant impact on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports recovered, but earlier market volatility caused by concerns over possible policy changes under the new US administration—including currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields across the region—only gradually stabilised at the beginning of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces have increased. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation and heightened financial market volatility could lead to tighter financial conditions. Meanwhile, the United States may pursue protectionist policies, which could affect regional economies, although the actual impact remains unclear. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private-sector business spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainty remains over the Mainland’s growth outlook. In particular, given the government’s determination to curb rising housing prices, the property sector’s contribution to growth may diminish this year if the property market continues to cool. Meanwhile, the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations may add uncertainty to the near-term economic outlook. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private-sector economic activity, some concerns remain in the market regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly in view of the acceleration in M1 growth alongside a slowdown in M2 growth. Box 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) explores the factors that may have caused the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate that there is no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the markedly faster growth of M1 than M2 is mainly attributable to monetary easing in recent years, which has lowered the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, as well as increased economic uncertainty, which may have boosted precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real Gross Domestic Product growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. On the domestic front, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. On the external front, growth in exports of goods increased as regional trade flows improved, while exports of services grew steadily with the recovery in trade-related and transportation services. As imports of goods and services grew more rapidly, net exports continued to weigh on real Gross Domestic Product growth in the second half of the year. As economic growth picked up, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. The Government and market consensus forecasts for real Gross Domestic Product growth in 2017 are 2–3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook continues to face significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong’s external demand. Amid appreciation pressure on the US dollar and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to become less supportive of the real economy and could lead to tighter domestic financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index to facilitate the monitoring of domestic financial conditions. Domestic inflationary pressures have remained moderate since the second half of 2016, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum accelerated slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rents. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, although it weakened intermittently following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered. As the US dollar appreciated, the nominal effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar rose further. Given the large Monetary Base, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, but rose from October onwards due to year-end funding demand and the need to catch up with the US dollar interest rate hike. As a result, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage rate edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by stronger domestic economic activity and increased year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Growth in domestic loans accelerated slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after declining modestly in the first half of the year. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio declined markedly to 63.8% on strong growth in US dollar deposits. Amid US dollar strength, both the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this background, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool, comprising customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit, consolidated further along with other offshore renminbi markets, while volatility in the offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate increased significantly. Nevertheless, banks’ renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds arising from uncertainty over movements in the renminbi exchange rate. With improving global market conditions, the Hong Kong stock market closed substantially higher during the review period. Although the US presidential election produced an unexpected result, the market experienced only a brief shock. This was mainly because investors’ expectations of fiscal stimulus measures under the Trump administration drove global equity markets higher. Although the local market benefited from this, its optimism was tempered by caution, possibly reflecting concerns over a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland’s economic outlook, uncertainty over renminbi policy and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply towards the end of last year and their spreads over US Treasury yields widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the review period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, although new bond issuance for the year as a whole was lower than in the previous year. Looking ahead, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets would come under pressure if global investors reverse their earlier search-for-yield strategies. With US trade policy still unclear and the renminbi exchange rate likely to remain volatile, the outlook for both bond markets over the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties. Following the Government’s introduction of the new stamp duty measure, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. In view of renewed market exuberance, the Government raised the stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets declined over the following two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting developers’ increased launches of primary-market residential projects. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, although the pace of increase moderated.

Following Donald Trump’s unexpected election as President of the United States, uncertainty over US policies increased. Although market attention has focused on the short-term benefits of potentially large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is already close to its potential, and fiscal stimulus may provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth while further intensifying upside risks to inflation. More importantly, risks facing emerging market economies are increasing amid capital outflow pressures arising from a faster pace of US interest rate increases and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures will also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes also increased recently. Nevertheless, against the backdrop of US interest rate increases, US dollar appreciation and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, with rising downside risks to economic growth. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated marginally in the second half of 2016 amid robust infrastructure investment growth and improving private-sector business spending. The Mainland economy continued to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing structural adjustment of the economy and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty over the near-term economic outlook. Given the Government’s determination to curb increases in housing prices, the property sector’s contribution to economic growth may also decline this year if the property market continues to cool. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 as the US dollar appreciated and US interest rates rose, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Global financial markets reacted strongly following Donald Trump’s unexpected election as US President. In particular, market expectations that Trump’s proposed policies, including tax reform, a large increase in infrastructure spending and deregulation, would boost US economic growth and inflation drove up major equity markets (Chart 2.1). Consequently, heightened market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate increases led to a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and a strengthening US dollar. Chart 2.1 Equity market indices in selected advanced economies Nevertheless, Trump’s anticipated tax cuts may not have as positive an impact on US economic growth as the market expects. Although shifting economic policy towards reliance on fiscal easing would help relieve the heavy burden borne by monetary easing, whether this is an appropriate time to implement fiscal easing is debatable given the current stage of the US economic cycle. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, and the unemployment rate in February was in line with the Federal Reserve’s estimate of the natural rate of unemployment of 4.7%, indicating that US economic activity is close to its potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary phase, during which the fiscal multiplier would be lower than in a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. Indeed, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital may result in lower tax revenue (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any event, with excess capacity diminishing, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on growth is limited, may push up inflation. Meanwhile, other factors, such as rising oil and commodity prices and potential trade protectionist measures, including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may also intensify upside risks to US inflation. Despite the increased risk of higher US inflation, the Federal Reserve remains cautious about tightening US monetary policy and is inclined to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market projections for the future federal funds rate have been revised upwards to levels close to the median of the Federal Reserve’s projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Federal Reserve’s longer-run projection (Chart 2.2). Thus, a faster pace of US interest rate increases could trigger significant market volatility. Although financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of stronger US economic growth driven by potentially expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, longer-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further increase in US government debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfil its campaign promises by adopting trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would create market distortions that undermine overall welfare, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Projections for the future federal funds rate: Federal Reserve versus market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and impediment to the European economic recovery. Although economic conditions in the euro area have gradually improved, with real gross domestic product growing moderately by 1.7% year on year in the fourth quarter, only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, economic activity in the euro area remains only slightly above its pre-global-financial-crisis level, compared with the stronger recovery in the US economy (Chart 2.3). Since the United Kingdom’s decision to leave the European Union last summer, markets have been concerned that the euro area may ultimately disintegrate. Although Italy’s economic and political situation appears to have stabilised after the formation of a new government and the implementation of measures to rescue its banking sector, forthcoming elections in Germany and France, and possibly Italy, could become political flashpoints amid Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly because of increased political uncertainty, European sovereign bond yields have continued to climb, while corporate bond spreads have also widened, particularly in peripheral countries. This could create a vicious cycle affecting the real economy and put pressure on real business investment in the euro area. Chart 2.3 Real gross domestic product in major advanced economies In Japan, real gross domestic product for recent quarters was revised upwards, with year-on-year growth rising to 1.6% in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger economic recovery than previously expected. However, partly because of structural problems in the labour market, slow wage growth has resulted in weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen means that the downward pressure exerted by the earlier appreciation of the yen on “new core” goods inflation is about to begin easing. Together with the stronger-than-expected recovery, this suggests an improved near-term inflation outlook, and “new core” inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, is expected to bottom out and recover after falling to 0.1% in December. Nevertheless, amid long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, while inflation expectations remain at around 0.5%–0.6%, below their level when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014. The risk therefore remains that inflation will fail to reach the Bank of Japan’s medium-term target of 2%. For other countries, particularly emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth transmitted through the trade channel may be smaller because of reduced US imports following the global financial crisis and the possibility that the US will implement protectionist policies. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate increases and further US dollar appreciation will tighten financial conditions and intensify downside risks to the economy. This may weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, together with concerns over a sharp rise in energy prices, led to a repricing of inflation risk, resulting in broad-based and significant increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of expectations of US interest rate increases on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with modest regional GDP growth and rising inflation. Real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable, supported by steady private consumption in a number of regional economies. Meanwhile, exports generally rose modestly from their 2015 lows. This reflected not only the stabilisation of growth in China, but also improved performance in advanced economies such as the United States and Europe. For net commodity exporters such as Malaysia and Indonesia, the recovery in commodity prices provided an additional boost. Other major exporters, such as South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, also regained momentum on growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — With the recovery in commodity prices, particularly oil prices, producer price inflation generally trended upwards. Although this will raise industrial costs and possibly consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may improve as the risk of prolonged deflation recedes. Faster producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, although the actual impact will depend on the extent to which increases in producer prices are passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the Consumer Price Index indicate that inflation in a number of regional economies, while still slightly below their respective central banks’ inflation targets for 2017, will rise closer to target levels (Chart 2.4). Except for Indonesia, central banks in East Asia generally maintained unchanged interest rates and accommodative monetary policies, while Indonesia cut interest rates twice, in September and October last year, to support growth. Chart 2.4 Headline Consumer Price Index inflation, forecasts and central bank targets in East Asia Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign exchange markets — Following the US presidential election, most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar as investors expected higher US inflation. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies depreciated less or even appreciated slightly following the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Post-US-election spot foreign exchange depreciation against the US dollar versus changes in nominal effective exchange rates Bond and equity markets — Asset prices declined briefly following the US presidential election but soon stabilised. Spreads between the sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasuries increased. However, as markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined, although they had yet to return to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed from their pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign bonds and US Treasuries Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the “taper tantrum” in mid-2013. Inflows resumed in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain stable, although still below its historical average. With increased uncertainty over US government policies and the Federal Reserve’s possible policy response, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. A sharp rise in the US dollar and yields may attract funds from the region to the United States, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, particularly those that are already highly valued. The resulting tightening of financial conditions would also create repayment pressure for corporations with large amounts of US-dollar-denominated debt. From a macroeconomic perspective, a broad-based rise in global interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which would not only weigh on aggregate demand in the short term but could also affect potential growth over the longer term. Finally, regional exporters face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies by the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in the region’s major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, clothing and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these industries have been accompanied by substantial job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalising US manufacturing could pose significant risks to regional exporters.

Faster growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activity led to a slight acceleration in Hong Kong’s economic growth in the second half of 2016. With the external environment becoming increasingly uncertain, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong’s economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew by 1.2% quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly faster than the 0.8% growth recorded in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly owing to improved consumer confidence and stable labour market conditions, private consumption growth accelerated and became the main driver of gross domestic product growth. Building and construction activity also became buoyant, supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport. However, weak corporate capital expenditure narrowed the contribution of overall investment spending to gross domestic product growth. On the external front, both imports and exports of goods grew at a faster pace alongside increased regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).22 Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded, partly because of strong travel demand among local residents. Net exports continued to drag on gross domestic product growth. Chart 3.1 Real Gross Domestic Product Growth and Contributions from Major Expenditure Components Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates in several major sectors declined during the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector showed signs of stabilising. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment Rate and Total Employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, amid uncertainty in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, growth in the global economy and trade may remain moderate. In addition, the rise in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar resulting from the strong US dollar will constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. On the domestic front, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately as it is weighed down by rising interest rates. Building and construction activity should grow steadily as housing supply increases and several planned infrastructure projects commence, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will restrain corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 2% and 3% in 2017, while the average forecast of private-sector analysts is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those arising from the external environment. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, with potential protectionist trade policies posing headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and general elections in several major European countries may also cause volatility in asset markets and affect Hong Kong dollar fund flows. In addition, US interest-rate normalisation will tighten domestic monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although the quarter-on-quarter momentum of domestic inflation has increased in recent months, inflation has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 through January this year (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before edging down to 2.4% in January. The increase in inflation momentum was mainly attributable to rises in tradable goods prices and housing rents (Chart 3.5). In particular, inflation in tradable goods prices rose from negative territory in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by prices of basic foodstuffs and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, the housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index increased as the decline in private residential rents narrowed and public housing rents were raised in September 2016, but subsequently slowed slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different Indicators of Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer Price Inflation by Major Component Chart 3.6 Rental Component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and Market Rents In the short term, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained owing to weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures. As the strength of the Hong Kong dollar offsets to some extent the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help ease business cost pressures and thereby restrain inflation in the services components. Despite the tight labour market, wage growth was modest in recent quarters. Real wages per employee rose by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against the backdrop of cautious business sentiment resulting from persistent uncertainty in the external environment, increases in labour costs should be restrained. In addition, given the weak performance of retail sales in recent months, growth in retail property rents is expected to be moderate. Moreover, the impact of the earlier easing in private residential rents will gradually emerge, which will also help alleviate inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline for 2017 as a whole. The Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the full year, lower than the 2.3% recorded in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and Import Prices Chart 3.8 Unit Labour Costs and Real Wages per Employee The inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation in the United States accelerates under the Trump administration, US interest-rate increases may occur at a faster-than-expected pace, potentially pushing up domestic mortgage rates and adding to downward pressure on property prices and housing rents. Meanwhile, appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may cause import prices to remain weak while also diminishing Hong Kong’s appeal to inbound visitors. On the upside, if the global economy expands faster than expected, Hong Kong’s economic growth may accelerate and demand-driven international commodity prices may rise, thereby creating upward pressure on domestic inflation. In addition, the increased statutory minimum wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which may push inflation higher, although the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank interest rates. Partly due to improvements in the domestic economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalization, uncertainty over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to a broad decline in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13–14, 2016 heightened market expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate increases, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened along with other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening as market expectations of a US interest rate increase in March rose from mid-February onward. The Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during the reporting period (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators Along with the strength of the US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar rose by 4.9% between August and December before stabilizing more recently (Chart 4.3). As the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners had only a modest impact, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance-of-payments statistics show that non-residents’ investment in equities and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and substantial initial public offering activity (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by increased holdings of US bonds by Hong Kong banks, residents’ debt investment recorded substantial outflows, which outweighed non-residents’ investment inflows. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated portfolio investment outflows in the final quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, coupled with expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate increases, put pressure on the local financial market and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data indicate that Hong Kong portfolio investment experienced inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly because investor optimism over the adoption of expansionary fiscal policies in the US improved global financial market performance. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalization would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states may increase fund-flow volatility. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading exceeded southbound trading in the initial period after the launch of Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained substantial and rose by a further 1.7% in the second half, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Of this amount, the Aggregate Balance contracted and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly as an additional HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills were issued to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base As domestic economic activity became more robust, growth in the Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half to 6.5% in the second half. As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand arising from stronger domestic economic activity and a rebound in initial public offering activity. Analyzed by counterpart assets, growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), representing respectively money created through credit expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded a higher increase of 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). By contrast, deposits in other foreign currencies contracted by a further 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, growth in total deposits at authorized institutions increased to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, while full-year growth was 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalization, banks’ wholesale funding costs rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, they increased partly because of year-end funding demand and the need to catch up with increases in US dollar interbank interest rates. Overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half, to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward in tandem with the US dollar yield curve, with the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at the end of December. At the beginning of 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined as funding demand eased, while longer-term Hong Kong Government Bond yields also edged down along with US Treasury yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates and the 10-year Government Bond yield Given the banking system’s large deposit base, increases in retail interest rates were relatively modest. Banks’ average funding costs, as measured by the composite interest rate, remained low, edging up by only 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). Owing to relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage business, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 in tandem with Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average interest rate on new mortgage loans Looking ahead, the pace of increases in domestic interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalization, the scale of capital outflows, and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on domestic interest rates, together with appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar’s real effective exchange rate in tandem with the US dollar, may reduce the support provided by domestic financial conditions to the real economy. Box 4 discusses the compilation of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index for monitoring domestic financial conditions. Driven by stronger domestic economic activity and increased demand for cross-border financing, total loans rose by a further 4.2% in the second half after growing by 2.2% in the first half (Chart 4.10). As economic growth momentum strengthened, growth in domestic loans accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after declining slightly in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Analyzed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also recorded moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. Total loans grew moderately by 6.5% for 2016 as a whole, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analyzed by economic sector, the performance of domestic loans was mixed in the second half (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial and finance-related enterprises and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, reflecting to some extent strong financing demand driven by better growth prospects in these sectors. Growth in loans for construction and property development also accelerated alongside increased private-sector construction activity. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade finance and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale, and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans to selected sectors Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half, compared with 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, rose by 7.2%, partly reflecting improvements in the economic environment (Chart 4.11), while growth in residential mortgage loans accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting buoyant residential property transactions between July and October. As a result, the household debt-to-GDP ratio also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt-to-GDP ratio and its components Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly stable. Reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at the end of June 2016 to 77.1% at year-end (Chart 4.13); meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at year-end, with the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio declining markedly to 63.8% owing to strong growth in US dollar deposits. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit ratios Given expectations of rising interest rates and the rapidly changing macro-financial environment, credit growth will be subject to uncertainty in the period ahead. The HKMA’s “Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook” indicates that loan demand will remain soft in the near term. Both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened as the US dollar appreciated (Chart 4.14). For most of late 2016, the offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi, closing at a yearly low of 6.98 against the US dollar at the end of 2016. The offshore renminbi interbank market again experienced liquidity-tightening pressure in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary funding demand ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid worsening market sentiment, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate surged to as high as 61.3% on January 6, 2017. The subsequent rise in offshore renminbi funding costs led to the unwinding of offshore renminbi short positions, driving a rebound in the offshore renminbi exchange rate in early January 2017, while the offshore-onshore renminbi differential also shifted to a premium. Since mid-January, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilized somewhat, liquidity conditions have gradually improved, and the overnight and three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates declined to 2.00% and 4.61%, respectively, at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared with the same period in 2015, owing to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decline in loan impairment charges. Banks’ capital positions and asset quality also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose notably following the US interest rate increase in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained favorable. Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable and low, underpinned by their large retail deposit base. Nevertheless, banks should prudently assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate increases, particularly the risk of substantial fund outflows and their subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. In addition, given the continued rise in the leverage of non-local corporates, a sharp increase in interest rates could lead to deterioration in banks’ asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be raised to 1.875% with effect from 1 January 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (the red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was attributable to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decline in loan impairment charges. For 2016 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose from 1.05% for 2015 as a whole to 1.10%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Retail banks’ net interest margin continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Hong Kong’s wholesale funding costs rose notably following the resumption of US interest rate increases in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose markedly by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained low by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates Nevertheless, the overall impact of the US interest rate increase on retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained modest. This was because retail deposits were retail banks’ primary source of funding, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low even after the interest rate increase. Under these circumstances, after remaining at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding costs, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016. More broadly, the aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar pattern. Although banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in average deposit funding costs in the retail market was smaller, at only 11 basis points. Overall, licensed banks’ average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 17 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Licensed banks’ Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by more and at a faster pace than Hong Kong banks’ funding costs, which could benefit some retail banks. This is because they had actively promoted mortgage loans priced with reference to the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate over the past few years, and increases in the interest rates on such loans could help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there were signs that some banks had narrowed the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. Over the longer term, as the US further raises interest rates, banks may soon face pressure to increase retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and having a more significant impact on net interest margins. Banks’ capital levels remained strong and well above the international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained high at 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated position. 2. The revised Basel III capital adequacy framework applicable to locally incorporated authorized institutions took effect on 1 January 2013. Therefore, capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onward are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. As measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained favorable during the reporting period. Although the average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions edged down from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016 to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016, it remained high (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained well above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that Hong Kong’s banking sector was capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for retail banks. The share of customer deposits in banks’ total liabilities rose from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks As retail banks’ total loans and advances and total deposits grew at similar rates during the reporting period, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). Over the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratios for Hong Kong dollars and foreign currencies also remained broadly unchanged. Chart 5.8 Retail banks’ average loan-to-deposit ratio Although locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate risk exposure increased slightly, it remained at a low level. Estimates indicate that, assuming a shock involving a general increase of 200 basis points in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base in December 2016 (Chart 5.9). Nevertheless, given that the pace of US interest rate normalization could be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the implications of this scenario for their interest rate risk management. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to its effect on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of a bank’s total capital base. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail banks’ loan portfolios remained sound. At the end of December 2016, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio remained low at 0.72% and 0.53%, respectively. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks Although current asset quality remained sound by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to monitor the external environment. As the assessment in Box 5 shows, the rapid growth since the global financial crisis in banking-sector loans for use outside Hong Kong indicates that banks’ asset quality has become more susceptible to the external environment. Banks had mixed expectations regarding short-term credit growth. The HKMA’s December 2016 “Survey on Credit Condition Outlook” showed that, although most authorized institutions surveyed expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the proportion expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk of unsecured personal loans remained manageable, with the annualized credit card charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24%, respectively, at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio for credit card lending, and bankruptcy petitions Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at the end of December. The average loan-to-value ratio for newly approved mortgages was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio was well below the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt-servicing index for new mortgages47 rose from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (the red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average size of new mortgage loans (Chart 5.13). Continued interest rate normalization in the US could further increase the household debt-servicing burden. A sensitivity test showed that, if interest rates rose by 300 basis points with other conditions unchanged, the index could increase significantly to 67.3 within four quarters.48 Banks should remain vigilant against the risks associated with the continued increase in the household debt-servicing burden. Chart 5.12 Average loan-to-value ratio for new mortgage loans and household debt-servicing burden Chart 5.13 New mortgage loans of surveyed authorized institutions The pace of US interest rate increases remained a key factor affecting the credit risk of corporate lending. However, the actual impact on the asset quality of individual banks depends on the characteristics of their corporate loan portfolios. In particular, our assessment based on the accounting data of non-financial companies listed in Hong Kong found that the leverage ratios of local and non-local corporates had exhibited markedly divergent trends since the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates more vulnerable to debt-servicing problems.50 Banks should assess the impact of interest rate increases on the credit risk of lending to non-local corporates. Specifically, corporate leverage, as measured by the weighted average debt-to-equity ratio, increased after the global financial crisis, with the increase mainly driven by non-local corporates. The leverage ratio of non-local corporates rose to 85% in the first half of 2016 (the red line in Chart 5.14), while that of local corporates remained broadly stable. As markets reassessed US inflation risks, volatility returned to global financial markets at the beginning of the year. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their end-January highs, fully offsetting the notable gains recorded at the beginning of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rise in global equity markets amid low volatility over the past two years was underpinned by market expectations of a benign economic environment featuring continued solid growth and persistently low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations are being challenged by the risks of tightening global monetary conditions, rising protectionist sentiment and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while markets continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. Both housing price growth and transaction volume rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017 after moderating slightly around the middle of last year. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in fund flows in Hong Kong. Given financial market uncertainties, the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against the risks of greater interest-rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) had hovered at low levels for more than two years, volatility returned to global financial markets at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their end-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point dropping by more than 10%, fully offsetting the notable gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was triggered by signs that the global economic recovery might exert pressure on long-subdued US wages and prices, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate the pace of interest-rate increases. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global equity markets over the past two years was founded on market expectations that benign economic conditions would persist. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with a synchronised pick-up in economic activity across advanced and emerging market economies. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and individual tax rules, raising market expectations that the strong US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite stronger activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rallied significantly in 2017, with US equity markets in particular repeatedly reaching new highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility subsides, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its potential output, and the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more rapidly. Meanwhile, as the tax cuts will result in a larger fiscal deficit, the US may issue more Treasury securities in the future, which is expected to increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to normalise its balance sheet. Outside the US, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would result in synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given the above uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, the sustainability of the current elevated valuations in global asset markets is in question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical expansion in global demand and the expected increase in the US fiscal deficit resulting from tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); in addition, the Federal Reserve’s balance-sheet normalisation is expected to raise the term premium, which may push up long-term interest rates and thereby weigh on asset market valuations. In East Asia, the region’s economies also enjoyed a benign environment of solid growth and moderate inflation. Alongside favourable economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows accelerated and financial markets rallied in tandem. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks from a number of factors, including tightening global liquidity as major central banks proceed with monetary policy normalisation in tandem; the US government’s pursuit of inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and the possibility of tighter offshore US dollar liquidity as US companies repatriate profits on a large scale in response to the one-off “deemed repatriation” provision under the US tax reform. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being most vulnerable to tighter financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by solid consumption, strong infrastructure investment and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. Meanwhile, signs of the emergence of the “new economy” became increasingly evident, with sectors such as high-value-added manufacturing and services displaying strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the “new economy” can help offset the near-term pressure on growth arising from further structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced that they would maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance in 2018, which may help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in both structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks’ exposures to companies in industries with excess capacity remained under control, while shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis also indicates that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity appear to have tightened, possibly because of reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017 amid stabilising economic conditions and diminishing risks. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real gross domestic product grew by 3.8% for 2017 as a whole, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow solidly in the second half of 2017. Overall investment expenditure also rebounded on the back of increased corporate capital spending. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to detract from gross domestic product growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018, supported by private consumption, building and construction activity, and exports. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government and the market consensus forecast real gross domestic product growth of 3–4% and 3.0%, respectively, in 2018. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, Mainland China’s economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and movements in the local asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a nearly 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained contained. However, there have been signs of a slight increase in quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum in recent months, with prices of both tradable goods and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up to a still-moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through of increases in newly contracted private residential rents. Driven by funding demand from initial public offerings and seasonal funding needs, tighter liquidity conditions and increased unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest-rate arbitrage activities revived, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened again from December 2017 onwards. At the beginning of 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates came under upward pressure between September and December 2017. This mainly reflected funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent approach to liquidity management towards the year end. In December, the average overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates were 0.25% and 1.26%, respectively, up by 14 and 50 basis points from six months earlier. After edging down in early January 2018, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained broadly stable and were unaffected by the recent correction in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans extended by banks followed the rise in short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, increasing to 2.16% in December. Meanwhile, retail banks’ funding costs remained generally low after a temporary rise in October due to initial public offering activities, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy continues to normalise; volatility in fund flows may also increase if global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly. For 2017 as a whole, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. In particular, growth in domestic loans to most sectors and loans for use outside Hong Kong both declined. Growth in foreign currency loans slowed, partly because of higher US dollar funding costs. By contrast, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth amid favourable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio increased in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% at year end, its highest level since March 2015. Meanwhile, owing to the relatively slow growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at year end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Thereafter, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, both the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool, comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit, edged up in the second half after declining slightly in the first half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi businesses, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the value of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong rebounded in the second half. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects drove global equity markets steadily higher in 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking the end of the calm conditions in financial markets over the previous two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tightening global financial conditions, together with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. Against the backdrop of a tight labor market, US tax cuts may accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Federal Reserve continues to normalize its balance sheet, increased US Treasury issuance to finance the tax cuts may add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The specter of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, supported by strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. However, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces various downside risks, including a potentially greater-than-expected tightening in global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialize, the risk of a reversal in capital flows would also increase. Policymakers face multiple challenges: on the one hand, they must guard against risks to economic growth; on the other, they must also contain the effects of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance-sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and in containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, partly depending on the extent to which the rapid growth of the “new economy” can offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilized and risks subsided, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the cyclical economic upturn that began in late 2016 became increasingly entrenched, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, investment and exports in the United States rose steadily, supported by improved private-sector sentiment and a substantial depreciation of the US dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilization of global commodity prices and stronger import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from corporate and personal income tax relief. In view of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated approximately 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Forecasts of real gross domestic product growth As growth momentum strengthened in the euro area and Japan, market expectations that the divergence in global monetary policies would narrow, together with a more optimistic global growth outlook, stimulated risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite three interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve during the year and the commencement of balance-sheet normalization, the US Dollar Index still fell by nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite a broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in the major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks’ targets, leading markets, until recently, to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly reaching record highs and pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the “dot-com bubble” in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher fiscal deficits and inflation have caused long-term US Treasury yields to rise steadily, raising questions about the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset-market valuations. As US average hourly earnings growth for January 2018 exceeded expectations, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index at one point fell by more than 10% from its January 26 peak, fully erasing its significant gains since the beginning of the year, and remained under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index at one point soaring to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the low-volatility environment that had prevailed over the previous two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, after the short-term equity-market volatility subsides, US inflation risks, upside risks to US long-term bond yields, and possible monetary tightening by other major central banks could all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform includes provisions expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The principal measures under the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing the full expensing of capital investment; and (3) a one-time “deemed repatriation” provision that helps reduce the incentive for US corporations to keep their overseas earnings offshore. Although it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its potential output, the tax cuts could push US output above potential, thereby causing the economy to overheat and inflation to rebound cyclically. If inflationary pressures rise by more than expected, the Federal Reserve may be prompted to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. At present, the path of the federal funds rate expected by financial markets is flatter than the projections released by the Federal Reserve. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden repricing of interest rate increase expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4).
