Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate projections Second, given that the tax reform may widen the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase in the future. As the Federal Reserve continues to implement its balance-sheet normalization plan, the term premium is expected to rise; under these circumstances, increased US Treasury issuance may intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. In addition, as market expectations of the passage of the US tax-cut package increased, US inflation expectations have continued to rise since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns about increased Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 Five-year, five-year forward inflation expectations Moreover, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for an extended period, as widely expected. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed to have fallen substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, US R* may face upside risks in the future because (1) an expected increase in the fiscal deficit would lower the national saving rate, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment of capital expenditure may raise the investment rate. A rise in R*, together with the expected increase in the term premium resulting from the Federal Reserve’s balance-sheet normalization, may signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset-market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, stronger growth momentum in the euro area and Japan has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back monetary accommodation. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening in global monetary conditions. In the euro area, member economies recorded broad-based cyclical expansions (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real gross domestic product recording an eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan have continued to signal that they will maintain accommodative monetary policies amid subdued inflation, the brighter growth outlooks in Europe and Japan, together with the continued tightening of Japan’s labor market, have led some market participants to predict further reductions in their quantitative easing programs in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real gross domestic product in selected euro-area member states Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent recovery in global economic growth and trade. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries. Recent examples include the announcement in January 2018 of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines, and the announcement in early March of import tariffs on steel and aluminum, raising concerns that its trading partners may respond with retaliatory measures. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom and other European Union countries are currently negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process fraught with uncertainty. If these developments lead to greater trade friction, they could impede global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions, such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East, or latent risks of terrorist attacks, could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a strong note. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided steady support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted the region’s exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressures have so far remained subdued. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated amid lower food-price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation, excluding food and energy, remained low due to sluggish wage growth in several economies. Chart 2.9 East Asia: Headline and core consumer price inflation* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and respective central banks. The improving economy, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, led to significant increases in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Capital inflows into regional markets rebounded markedly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose with the markets. Indeed, credit risk premiums in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Hong Kong’s economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew by 0.8% quarter on quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was robust because of favourable employment and income conditions, continued optimism in consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activity weakened, increased corporate capital expenditure led overall investment spending to rise markedly in the final quarter after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions from major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment increased by about 0.7% to more than 3.85 million, with the most notable increases in construction, financial and business services, and public administration, social and personal services. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance will continue to benefit from an improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly because of favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. As for domestic gross fixed capital formation, building and construction activity should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. Although an improving economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, possible interest rate increases may have an adverse impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3% to 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts by international organisations and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in the preceding chapters, the performance of the Mainland Chinese economy amid tightening financial conditions, and developments in Hong Kong’s asset markets. Domestic inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although sequential inflation momentum showed signs of a slight pick-up in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The rebound in newly contracted private residential rents since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.5 Unit labour costs and salaries per capita As global inflation remains moderate and increases in domestic costs are stable, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate may gradually rebound from the eight-year low of 1.7% recorded in 2017. For example, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 because of the pass-through effect from growth in newly contracted private residential rents. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2018 is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, any larger-than-expected rise in global inflation or commodity prices could increase domestic inflation momentum. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, falling below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a substantial tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the low interest rate environment after the 2008 global financial crisis, Hong Kong households’ mortgage indebtedness increased. As US dollar interest rate normalisation progresses, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise in tandem with US dollar interest rates, correspondingly increasing households’ mortgage repayment burden in the future and thereby weighing on household consumption. This box therefore examines the impact of an increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the proportion of income accounted for by mortgage debt-service payments, namely interest payments plus repayments of loan principal. Chart B3.1 shows the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect and income effect commonly cited in economic theory, as well as the wealth effect and collateral effect arising from changes in asset prices, where there is a mortgage repayment burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and, in turn, households’ disposable income. This impact will increase as the amount of outstanding mortgage loans rises. Moreover, repayments of loan principal vary with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, which also affects private consumption by changing households’ disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the outstanding mortgage debt-service-to-income ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the current mortgage repayment burden indicator, which applies only to newly originated mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding household mortgage debt, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the aggregate income of owner-occupier households, proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households, and rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows estimates of the OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population censuses. In the early 2000s, both ratios trended downward, consistent with the decline in aggregate household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997 and the sharp fall in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite the substantial rise in property prices following the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable because the HKMA’s macroprudential measures on banks’ mortgage lending contained aggregate household mortgage leverage. In addition, the extension of maturities for newly originated mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income We also compare the OMDSR with banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which is the actual debt-service-to-income ratio of banks’ applicants for newly originated mortgages. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks’ debt-servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only newly originated mortgages but also existing mortgages. As property prices were lower when existing mortgages were originated, repayments on these mortgages are correspondingly lower than those on newly originated mortgages. Therefore, an outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and newly originated mortgages, namely the OMDSR, will be lower than an indicator of the repayment burden on newly originated mortgages, namely banks’ debt-servicing ratio. In addition, banks’ debt-servicing ratio is higher because, in compliance with the HKMA’s prudential supervisory requirements, banks include repayments of non-mortgage loans when calculating the debt-servicing ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly because the HKMA’s prudential supervision of mortgage lending imposed a cap on banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio for newly originated mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used repayment burden indicators, but it is more timely and can reflect the burden of total outstanding mortgage debt rather than only that of newly originated mortgage debt. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In the model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption, proxied by real average private consumption per household, and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we use real income, proxied by median household income deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index; real housing and financial wealth, proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, both deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index; and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total loans continued to increase in the second half of 2017, although growth slowed from the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Volatility in fund flows may also increase if global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly and remained around 7.80 between September and November 2017. This mainly reflected increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end, which tightened liquidity conditions, in turn slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for US dollars increased, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate weakened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, but the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Indicators of fund flows The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and had only a limited impact on the Real Effective Exchange Rate Index, the Real Effective Exchange Rate Index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to closely track movements in the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics show that equity portfolio investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents’ debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows from residents’ debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017 amid market optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that despite corrections in global financial markets, equity investment continued to record inflows, while bond investment recorded slight fund outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalization continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, potentially leading to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given the uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalization and rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board arrangements. Despite the Federal Reserve’s interest rate increases and continued balance-sheet reduction, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by a further 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly due to growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued to back banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged in the second half, at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this amount, the Aggregate Balance declined, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills totaling HK$80 billion to meet banks’ substantial liquidity management demand. Entering 2018, the monetary base remained stable despite a correction in the equity market. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply increased further in the second half of 2017, although at a slower pace. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HK$M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As the main component of HK$M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly because buoyant asset markets increased investment demand. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that growth in HK$M3 was supported by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), but was dampened by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 HK$M3 and changes in its asset counterparts On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, growth in US dollar deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, after declining continuously for more than two years, other foreign currency deposits rebounded markedly by 8.4% in the second half. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in renminbi deposits. As growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with growth of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December on a monthly average basis. The negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates for tenors of one to three months narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly mirroring movements in the US dollar yield curve. During the second half, the yield on three-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on ten-year Hong Kong Government Bonds increased by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, the composite interest rate and the average interest rate on new mortgages Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates declined in early January. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained broadly stable. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks’ lending rates rose in tandem with the surge in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate, banks’ funding costs generally remained low because of the still-substantial deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks’ average interest rate on new mortgages gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the increase in the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. On the other hand, although the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs, briefly rose in October because of increased funding demand from initial public offerings, it remained subdued for most of the second half and closed at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize and other major economies may begin normalizing interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase volatility in fund flows. Nevertheless, the substantial Hong Kong dollar monetary base can serve as a buffer and help moderate an excessively rapid rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window will also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth was as high as 10.2% in the first half, but slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed. Analyzed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half amid favorable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Among these, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly because of rising US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong, including trade finance, declined from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Growth in loans for construction and property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities had required banks to strengthen risk management for lending to property developers since June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail sectors declined. By contrast, growth in loans to finance- and financial-related companies remained strong, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans to selected sectors Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, accelerated further to 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management clients secured by financial assets. Growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such secured loans were manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks in January 2014 on risk management for personal lending, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including imposing caps on loan tenors and borrowers’ debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volume increased, loan-to-value ratios for newly approved mortgages declined, and growth in residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Mainly benefiting from growth in net interest income, retail banks’ profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth slowed in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in the Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rate, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained low owing to low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should remain alert to the risks of increased interest-rate volatility and potential fund outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of a larger-than-expected increase in interest rates. To strengthen banks’ resilience against systemic risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 13.6% from the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a decrease in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as assets grew faster than earnings, retail banks’ return on assets edged down from 1.17% in the first half of 2017 to 1.15% in the second half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Figure 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 15.8%, while their return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Figure 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further from 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Figure 5.2). Observational evidence suggests that the improvement in the net interest margin was consistent with the increase in the average spread on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in Hong Kong’s syndicated loan market (Figure 5.3). Figure 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Figure 5.3 Average spread on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans Since September 2017, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates have risen across the board, mainly owing to liquidity demand associated with initial public offerings and banks’ liquidity needs towards year-end, as well as expectations of US interest-rate increases. In particular, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Figure 5.4). Entering 2018, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates appeared to stabilise as banks’ year-end liquidity needs eased. Despite the recent rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained stable. This was mainly attributable to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, which reflects retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds, remained low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up only recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Figure 5.4). A similar pattern was observed in licensed banks’ overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs. In the second half of 2017, banks’ average cost of non-deposit market funding in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 35 basis points, while their average deposit funding cost edged up by 12 basis points. Overall, licensed banks’ average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost increased by 22 basis points (red line in Figure 5.5). Figure 5.4 Interest rates Figure 5.5 Licensed banks’ Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities The rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates exceeded the increase in the banking sector’s overall funding costs, which may help improve banks’ interest margins on assets benchmarked against Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates. However, this improvement may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have narrowed the spread between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest-rate increases this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. In view of intense competition in the loan market, banks’ net interest margins could come under pressure if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that Hong Kong’s banking sector remained well capitalised. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased from 18.7% at the end of June to 19.1% (Figure 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Figure 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper on proposed rules prescribing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. Although enhancing authorized institutions’ loss-absorbing capacity would benefit society by helping reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis, it would inevitably also entail costs. Box 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing loss-absorbing capacity requirements would generate net benefits for the Hong Kong economy. As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions edged down from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that Hong Kong’s banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks’ medium- and long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of not less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system’s stable funding structure. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Figure 5.8). Figure 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Figure 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign-currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. Figure 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions Locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest-rate risk exposures remained low. We estimate that, under a hypothetical shock involving a 200-basis-point parallel rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest-rate positions would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Figure 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue raising interest rates and normalising its balance sheet, banks should assess the implications for their interest-rate risk management. Figure 5.10 Impact of an interest-rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, amid moderate but still favourable economic conditions, growth in the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3% from the robust 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of slowing growth, total loans recorded solid growth of 16.1% for 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% respectively at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Figure 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risks. Figure 5.11 Retail banks’ asset quality As banks became more optimistic about near-term credit growth, robust credit growth is expected to continue. The HKMA’s December 2017 Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook showed that 29% of the authorized institutions surveyed expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk associated with personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages declined further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA introduced the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures in September 2009.

The global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened amid increasing uncertainties arising from persistent trade frictions, tighter financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, stressing that decisions would be “data dependent” and that “patience” was needed, leading investors to rule out the possibility of further interest rate increases. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. Growth in total loans moderated slightly in the second half of 2018, reflecting weaker credit demand amid headwinds including the continuing US-China trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes falling markedly and housing prices declining, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s banking sector faces multiple headwinds due to increased uncertainties in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, they could significantly dampen business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact that a possible deterioration in the external environment could have on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The global economy continued to grow in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy expanded steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, growth decelerated in Japan and several major euro-area countries, while inflation remained subdued. Slowing global trade and a marked decline in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of weakening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, from its October 2018 projections. As the growth outlook dimmed and trade frictions intensified, global equity markets experienced sharp volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, triggering market concerns that the United States was approaching a recession. However, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term was low. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remained fraught with uncertainty. In the United States, although moderate inflation gave the Federal Reserve room to pause interest rate increases, the Fed’s data-dependent policy stance also suggested that financial markets could become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that might prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of US-China and US-European Union trade negotiations remained uncertain. In the United Kingdom, it remained unclear whether a solution to avoid a “hard Brexit” could be achieved. In East Asia, financial markets stabilised as the US dollar’s appreciation slowed and markets expected the Federal Reserve to pause interest rate increases, but a deterioration in the external environment could weigh on the region’s economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade growth had already dragged on growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures had also eased. Although this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks in balancing support for growth against curbing inflation, financial imbalances, including high private-sector indebtedness in some countries in the region, remained serious. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge confronting East Asia was that the impact of an unexpected change in the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy could spill over to the sovereign bond markets of emerging market economies, including those in East Asia. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 amid increased uncertainty in the external environment and a slight moderation in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remained uncertain as US-China trade negotiations had yet to reach a conclusion. A marked contraction in shadow financing had increased the financing difficulties faced by private enterprises, particularly small firms, over the past few quarters, while weakening economic confidence could also put pressure on business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers needed to continue striking a balance between stabilising the economy and preventing and controlling potential systemic risks by adopting accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted reductions in the reserve requirement ratio. Meanwhile, the authorities also introduced more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among firms under different forms of ownership, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0–6.5%. Risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets in 2018. Banks’ asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage of listed non-financial companies edged up. However, banks’ loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, and their exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline, with both developments helping to protect the banking system against a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage of listed companies in industries with excess capacity—one of the main sources of banks’ credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors contributing to the recent improvement in the business performance of industries with excess capacity. Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stalled and year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activity was mainly due to consumption and exports being adversely affected, directly or indirectly, by the US-China trade conflict. Slower growth in private consumption may have reflected increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect arising from corrections in local asset prices. On the external front, Hong Kong’s merchandise export performance also deteriorated, particularly after China and the United States implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the US-China trade conflict on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and explores the short-term outlook and related risks. Mainly due to slower global economic growth, economic growth was expected to decelerate further in 2019. Amid the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance was expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption was expected to continue supporting economic growth amid low unemployment and rising household income, but the outlook for overall investment spending could become more uncertain. The Government forecast real GDP growth of 2–3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts averaged 2.3%. These forecasts were subject to the various uncertainties and risks described above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation partly reflected earlier growth in newly contracted private residential rents. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years, growth in total employment showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures were expected to remain moderate in 2019 as domestic economic growth momentum weakened. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four more times in March 2019 (as of 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar depreciated against the US dollar, partly due to the rebuilding of carry-trade positions. Despite the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered again in March, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate increases. Compared with June 2018, the three-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by around 30 basis points to monthly averages of 2.32% and 2.74%, respectively, in December. Entering 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of September. At the end of January 2019, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans rose in tandem with best lending rates to around 2.45%. As uncertainties surrounding US-China trade frictions and Brexit negotiations persisted, volatility in fund flows could intensify. In addition, the sizeable negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar could stimulate arbitrage activity, leading to capital outflows. Under such circumstances, capital outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates had faced depreciation pressure amid market concerns over an escalation in US-China trade frictions. However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism generated by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the United States. Although US-China trade frictions persisted, they had not yet had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the three-month offshore renminbi interbank offered rate hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half, with renminbi customer deposits increasing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. Average daily turnover in the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite continuing concerns over US-China trade frictions, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to continue expanding, supported by the opening of the Mainland’s capital account, the development of stock and bond market connectivity, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. The local equity market experienced roller-coaster-like swings over the past six months. At the beginning of the review period, the market fell sharply due to continued US monetary policy tightening, major differences between the two sides in US-China trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in the Mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted to a “patient” monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade-war truce, China adopted further measures to reduce its trade surplus with the United States and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the United States brought a highly politicised legal prosecution against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides made conciliatory gestures, signalling their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local equity market rebounded sharply at the beginning of the year. However, considerable uncertainty remained as the two sides discussed the details of any agreement, while future developments in the US federal prosecution would complicate matters, particularly in the high-technology sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, and performance improved towards the end of the year as market expectations of a slower pace of US monetary policy normalisation strengthened. As a result, fund flows into bond funds reversed in the second half and registered a modest increase. Issuance in Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi market rebounded sharply after declining for three consecutive years. However, as Mainland companies continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below the amount of maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remained challenging, with its outlook depending on economic developments globally, particularly in the Mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened amid a combination of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly in regions outside the United States. In view of the dimmer growth outlook, the US Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be “data dependent” and that it would exercise “patience”, while no longer providing forward guidance on further interest rate increases. As the Fed’s policy stance becomes data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data and may perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainty over global trade policy and increased geopolitical risks may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since the end of 2018 amid signs that the US interest rate hike cycle was slowing and the US dollar was stabilising. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown because of a deteriorating external environment, namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weaker growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, while uncertainty over the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Policymakers therefore adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. In the face of these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and contain systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to register broad-based growth. However, although the US economy remained broadly robust, some signs of moderation emerged. There were also clear signs of weakening growth momentum outside the United States. Several country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian government bond yields amid a fiscal stand-off with the European Union, and social unrest in France, all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also created new challenges for commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for global growth in 2019 by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices of selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production in emerging market economies In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent a sharp correction amid slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, market concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Fed’s indication that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry that the United States was heading towards an imminent recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Treasury yields and probability of a US recession Nevertheless, the probability of a US recession in the near term is very low. US economic fundamentals remain robust, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, and economic overheating is unlikely to prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy substantially. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening in financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data dependent, noting that moderate inflationary pressures allowed them to exercise “patience” in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the US Federal Open Market Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further interest rate increases and announced that it “would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments”. This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World ex USA Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Fed’s recent “dovish” signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain and depends on inflation and other developments. Moderate inflationary pressures so far have given the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary policy normalisation. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that the Fed can exercise patience (Chart 2.5). In addition, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth outside the United States and trade policy uncertainty. In view of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations However, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which normally signals higher inflation ahead (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that essentially rule out a Fed interest rate increase in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds target range remaining unchanged in 2019 and of at least one interest rate increase Overall, a prolonged pause in interest rate increases by the Fed is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data dependent as a risk-management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that may prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the euro area, the European Central Bank ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, describing risks to the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside”. The implications of this downgrade to the ECB’s growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan stated at its latest policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary easing could be considerable, as its effectiveness has been questioned and the adverse effects of a prolonged ultra-low interest rate environment have become increasingly apparent. For example, the capital ratios of regional banks declined from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018, as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from uncertainties surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, uncertainty over the outcomes of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are also two major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. In early December, the US Government announced that it would refrain from increasing tariffs on imports from China for 90 days and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the United States and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. As the outcomes of these trade negotiations remain uncertain, they may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the United States, disagreements between the two parties over funding for border security led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives may lead to further policy gridlock in the future. In the United Kingdom, risks associated with Brexit and its spillover effects surged after the May government’s Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and it remains uncertain whether a plan can be formulated at the last minute to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit”. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as renewed US sanctions on Iran, may also create uncertainty over oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, after fluctuating during the first three quarters of last year, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter. The stabilisation of the US dollar since October and signs that the Fed would remain patient about further interest rate increases eased the depreciation and capital outflow pressures faced by East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio capital flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: currency index and capital flows Despite financial market stability, there are increasing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, regional export growth declined, causing real gross domestic product growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies, which reflect short-term external trade performance, have fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that short-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers’ Index new export orders indices for East Asian economies Amid slowing growth and the recent fall in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: headline inflation and oil prices As recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar have both been relatively moderate, East Asian central banks no longer face an urgent need to raise interest rates, easing the policy dilemma of balancing support for economic growth against curbing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private-sector indebtedness in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weaker export performance amid the US-China trade dispute. With global growth slowing, real gross domestic product (GDP) growth is also expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and economic performance in Mainland China. Local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019, with the outlook subject to both upside and downside risks. Economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to maintain the strong momentum of the first half, and quarter-on-quarter GDP growth turned slightly negative in the second half of the year (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the growth rate falling below trend growth to 1.3% in the fourth quarter, bringing full-year growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Calculated on the basis of the expenditure-based and seasonally adjusted volume index of GDP. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions from major expenditure components The weakening in economic activity was mainly attributable to the drag on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect effects of the US-China trade conflict. Growth in private consumption slowed, possibly because of increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect arising from corrections in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Gross investment expenditure declined markedly amid fragile business confidence. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after the US and China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance in greater detail and discusses its near-term outlook and related risks. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports With economic activity weakening, employment growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to approximately 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. With output and employment growth remaining weak, labour productivity was broadly stable, showing no signs of substantial improvement. As global economic growth slows further, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. In the face of a challenging external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the domestic front, although the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, growth in private consumption is expected to moderate, partly because of weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect caused by earlier corrections in asset prices. As for fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. Although building and construction activity is expected to continue growing steadily as housing supply increases, firms may become more cautious about capital investment as economic uncertainty rises. Business sentiment indicators, such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index, continued to hover in contractionary territory, and projections of future economic growth based on the index pointed to a further slowdown in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2–3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to the various uncertainties and risks described in the preceding two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures have continued to build in recent months, they remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half of the year. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by rises in certain service prices. Earlier increases in newly contracted private residential rents and faster rises in the prices of meals bought away from home continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures remained broadly moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.5 Unit labour costs and per capita payroll Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019. This mainly reflects weaker domestic growth momentum. However, earlier increases in private residential rents will continue to feed through to consumer price inflation. The consensus market forecast for the overall inflation rate for the year is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The inflation outlook described above is subject to both upside and downside risks. Regarding downside risks, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the currently near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if an easing of US-China trade frictions leads the local economy to perform better than expected, local inflation could be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The US-China trade conflict intensified progressively in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the US imposed additional tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China respectively. Immediately following these two measures, Mainland China responded by imposing additional tariffs of 25% on an equivalent value of US goods. The US escalated its measures further on 24 September by imposing additional tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing additional tariffs of 5–10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. Since then, the two countries have entered into negotiations to avoid further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the additional tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The US-China trade dispute therefore has important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify the traded goods directly affected by the additional tariffs, thereby examining their impact in greater detail. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extracted data on six groups of goods re-exported through Hong Kong that were respectively affected by the various rounds of additional tariffs described in the preceding section. In the first two rounds of tariff increases, the US imposed tariffs mainly on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China primarily targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods widened to include more consumer goods. For simplicity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of additional tariffs as List 1, List 2 and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus our analysis on year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. In addition, caution is required when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity during that month was disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of the additional tariffs. Hong Kong re-exports of Mainland origin affected by tariffs Shortly after the additional tariffs were imposed, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US through Hong Kong appeared to decline markedly or record slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 goods slowed in the first month after the tariffs were imposed, while re-exports of List 3 goods recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports of goods on all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US through Hong Kong in 2018 Hong Kong re-exports of US origin affected by tariffs By comparison, goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports of List 1 goods appeared to decline markedly in the few months after the tariffs were imposed, but recovered towards the end of the year. Re-exports of List 2 goods generally recorded negative growth throughout the year, while growth in List 3 goods appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong in 2018 Front-loading Since there is sometimes a time lag between the announcement and final implementation of tariffs (or simply because of the threat of tariff increases), firms may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected effective date of the tariffs. Indeed, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading was fairly widespread. Some private-sector analysts also believe that this behaviour partly explains the strength of the overall trade figures before the tariffs were imposed. The more granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for goods on certain tariff lists, but this appears to have involved only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 goods increased in the months before the respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, growth in re-exports from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong (Chart B3.2) showed no clear evidence of front-loading by firms. Hong Kong re-exports not affected by additional tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the additional tariffs accounted for only around 4–5% of the total value of Hong Kong’s re-exports. To gain a fuller understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, re-exports not affected by the additional tariffs should also be examined. We found that re-exports not affected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in both of the final two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). In addition, the decline in the growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) was noticeably greater from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in growth of re-exports not affected by the additional tariffs partly reflected a broader weakening in external demand. As ongoing trade frictions continue to increase uncertainty, global financial conditions tighten and geopolitical risks rise, external demand could come under more broad-based pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in corrections in major stock markets. Import demand from other economies has consequently been dampened, constraining Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Global growth is likely to slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is bound to further constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that firms of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trading sector particularly subdued.
