The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades as liquidity tightened amid expectations of seasonal funding demand. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly because corporations remitted back funds raised through initial public offerings and the market rebuilt carry-trade positions, triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before declining in January 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar fund flows may become more volatile amid uncertainties such as the ongoing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, market carry-trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until March 2019, when the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four more times in total (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again from November onwards, as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity and led to the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporations’ remittance back of funds raised through initial public offerings and the market’s rebuilding of carry-trade positions. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken gradually and triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance had remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), before declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion after the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March (as of 19 March). Hong Kong dollar fund outflows since April 2018 accounted for only a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion of inflows since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had only a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the latter broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates The latest balance-of-payments statistics show that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased stock market volatility, outflows of equity securities investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting portfolio investment inflows from non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both local residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, fund-flow volatility may intensify amid uncertainties such as the ongoing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry-trade activities and lead to fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are both part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation process and the repeated triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year to HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly attributable to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for broader measures of the Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainty in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HK$M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year, but increased only slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of HK$M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits were little changed compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly because of fewer investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit interest rates increased. An analysis of counterpart assets shows that the slower growth in HK$M3 was attributable to changes in banks’ capital and reserves (included under “net other items”). Chart 4.5 Changes in HK$M3 and its counterpart assets Foreign currency deposit growth accelerated in the second half of the year. As banks attracted more deposits after raising preferential US dollar deposit rates, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of growth in foreign currency deposits (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Despite the still-large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposit base, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank offered rates, causing them to be more volatile than longer-term interbank offered rates (Chart 4.7). Three-month and 12-month HIBOR averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, around 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Entering 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally declined as seasonal demand receded. The averages of three-month and 12-month HIBOR fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, yields on three-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average interest rate on new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, increased slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before declining to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September. However, retail banks made no further adjustments to their best lending rates after the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised again in December. Meanwhile, the average interest rate on new mortgages rose in tandem with best lending rates to around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, movements in US dollar interest rates, fund flows, and local financial market activities, such as initial public offering subscriptions, will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial amount of Exchange Fund Bills, the pace of increases in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate, as banks can use Exchange Fund Bills as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window. Against the backdrop of intensifying China-US trade tensions, both offshore and onshore renminbi depreciated against the US dollar from the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism arising from the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the United States. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates So far, the ongoing China-US trade tensions have not had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally because of seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). Three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting the monetary easing measures recently introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of developments in the China-US trade negotiations on liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Fixings of overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Within these deposits, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit declined by a further 14.1% in the second half, mainly because of reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and the relatively large amount of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Mainly benefiting from increased net interest income, retail banks’ profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar interbank rate and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalization, retail banks’ overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs increased notably, although they remained at a relatively low level. Against an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilizing from November onward, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from continued uncertainty over China-US trade relations, a slowdown in the global economy, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant regarding the impact that a possible further deterioration in the external environment may have on the credit risk associated with their corporate lending. Retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period of the previous year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Broadly reflecting further US interest rate increases and a decline in Hong Kong dollar interbank liquidity after the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to compete for stable, longer-term funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. In addition, following the US interest rate increase decision at the end of September, banks raised their best lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the increases in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding costs, rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, although it remained low by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs increased by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half of the year (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks The cumulative increase in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate exceeded the rise in banks’ overall funding costs in Hong Kong, which may have had a positive effect on retail banks’ HIBOR-based mortgage loans, a type of loan that the industry had actively promoted over the preceding years. However, further improvement in net interest margins may become more limited because most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached their best-lending-rate-based interest rate caps. As the timing of future increases in best lending rates remains uncertain, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid US interest rate normalization may weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment may cloud banks’ profitability outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, continued uncertainty over China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this results in a marked decline in lending and a deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks’ profitability. Hong Kong’s banking sector remained well capitalized, far above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions increased further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated position. 2. With effect from 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Accordingly, capital ratios from March 2013 onward are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, likewise well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated that authorized institutions had stable funding positions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also above the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. Authorized institutions’ ample liquidity and sound funding positions indicate that Hong Kong’s banking sector is capable of withstanding a range of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system’s stable funding structure. At the end of 2018, customer deposits as a proportion of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions edged up from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. By contrast, as Hong Kong dollar deposit growth was far lower than Hong Kong dollar loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. We estimate that, under a hypothetical across-the-board interest rate shock of 200 basis points, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate increases, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management.
