The interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard parallel interest rate shock of 200 basis points on institutions’ interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the effect on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. Against the backdrop of continued uncertainty over China-US trade conflicts, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed markedly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilizing from November 2018 onward. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic lending, including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2%, respectively, in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, total loan growth slowed markedly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the near term. The HKMA’s December 2018 Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that, among all surveyed authorized institutions, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of authorized institutions expecting demand to decline rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite the slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36%, respectively, at the end of December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40%, respectively, at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio declined slightly to 0.50%, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks 1. Classified loans refer to loans classified as “substandard,” “doubtful,” or “loss.” 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of retail banks’ Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onward, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include retail banks’ major overseas subsidiaries. On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to slower growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal gross domestic product grew more slowly than personal loans, the ratio of household debt to gross domestic product edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic impact of the outbreak, financial markets have remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance staying stable and total deposits growing moderately, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or Hong Kong’s banking system was observed during the review period. After rebounding moderately in the first half of 2019, growth in total loans slowed in the second half. The residential property market generally softened from mid-2019, although its movements were somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increases in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth had shown tentative signs of stabilisation, supported by increased monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of China-US trade tensions and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit” in the United Kingdom. However, the continued increase in coronavirus infections worldwide since late January has raised market concerns and triggered substantial volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks posed by the outbreak, several major central banks sharply cut interest rates and expanded their liquidity facilities, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp falls in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will dampen global economic activity, with the extent of the economic impact depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, tensions between the United States and its major trading partners may re-escalate, while the United Kingdom’s post-Brexit trade negotiations with the European Union may also be fraught with difficulties. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia1. East Asia’s exports to major destinations, including the United States, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but whether the technology product cycle is undergoing a broad-based recovery remains to be seen. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States announced in December 2019, and the trade truce reduced global trade uncertainty to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region may hurt Asia’s tourism industry, particularly economies that are more dependent on exports of tourism services. Given the region’s close supply-chain links with Mainland China, manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 owing to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States should temporarily reduce the external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressure remains amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made economic stability a priority for 2020 while also emphasising the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed to a possible decline in shareholders’ equity among private industrial enterprises in recent years, regarding it as a sign of a “private-sector retreat”. Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in the equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed-company data, and finds that private enterprises or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. Although the study finds that negative earnings are the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural factors, also warrant attention (see Box 2 for details). Economic activity in Hong Kong contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. Real gross domestic product declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weaker domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main drag on gross domestic product in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely disrupted consumption activity, leading to a weak economic outlook that in turn dampened consumer and business confidence. With the renewed escalation of China-US trade tensions, slower global economic growth and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued. In view of the strong headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater scope to step up support for the domestic economy and help moderate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks would be lowered from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity for businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the outbreak recently adding substantial downside risks. As industries such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism and transportation have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget may provide relief to households and businesses, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to businesses with a 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.2 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further lowered the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, giving banks greater scope to step up support for the domestic economy, particularly industries and individuals facing greater short-term pressure as a result of the outbreak. In terms of the components of gross domestic product, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak because of fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States is expected to have a slight positive impact on the domestic economy in the short term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while growth forecasts by international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, Mainland China’s economic performance and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising and the real wage index also falling year on year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate will rise further in view of the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 examines recent labour-market developments and the near-term outlook in greater detail. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly because of higher fresh pork prices; inflation momentum then gradually eased as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to moderate in the near term owing to weak economic conditions, the consolidation of private residential rents and moderate imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts for the headline inflation rate in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for Hong Kong dollars, including that arising from initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October 2019. Entering December, the appreciation momentum of the Hong Kong dollar strengthened further, partly because of buoyant initial public offering activity and partly because tighter liquidity towards year-end prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly during the review period, without triggering the Convertibility Undertaking. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates have fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital-market activity such as initial public offerings. Box 4 examines how market attention to forthcoming initial public offering activity affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest-rate caps linked to the best lending rate, the average interest rate on new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October. However, as best lending rates in the market were lowered from November onwards, the average interest rate on new mortgages edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance staying stable and total deposits growing moderately, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or Hong Kong’s banking system was observed during the review period. Nevertheless, it is necessary to monitor the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus outbreak amid uncertainties in the external environment. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to address capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, expectations of a China-US trade agreement strengthened both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates, although they came under weakening pressure following the coronavirus outbreak from late January 2020. In the latter part of 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi. The discount widened briefly at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a modest decline in the previous review period. At the end of January 2020, the balances of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion. Hong Kong’s other renminbi businesses also expanded, with strong growth recorded in local renminbi bank lending and renminbi trade settlement business. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion for 2019 as a whole. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, increased allocations to renminbi assets by international investors, and deeper regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes of a global economic recovery. However, the continued rise in global coronavirus infections since late January 2020 dashed hopes of a recovery and deepened investor concerns about a global recession, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To address the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. In view of the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has clouded the outlook for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism industry being particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 owing to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressure remains amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities’ monetary and fiscal policy responses will provide some cushion. Under the impact of persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was still sluggish in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, growth showed preliminary signs of stabilising in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier monetary easing by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US “Phase One” trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index However, since the end of January, the continued increase in global coronavirus infections and the ensuing economic shock have raised market concerns and triggered a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in global supply chains, disruptions to production activity in the Mainland and the resulting drag on its economic growth will generate significant spillovers that could spread globally (Chart 2.3). Since late February, coronavirus infections have surged outside Mainland China, potentially exacerbating supply-chain disruptions and posing the risk of a direct drag on local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and option-adjusted spread of the Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) In response to the potentially severe economic shock from the pandemic, some central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nevertheless, financial markets remain under enormous selling pressure, resulting in a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which may in turn intensify downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for advanced economies Apart from developments in the pandemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are not expected to proceed smoothly, thereby prolonging post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 owing to sluggish global demand. East Asia’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there were preliminary signs that the downturn in the regional technology-product cycle was bottoming out, including reports by major regional electronics companies of improved earnings at the end of 2019,6 it remains to be seen whether there has been a substantive rebound in regional technology-product exports. Chart 2.5 East Asia: merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region’s potential economic growth over the longer term. To support economic growth amid moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also reduced its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As several economies in the region have imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies more dependent on visitors from Mainland China and exports of travel services being more severely affected by the outbreak (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and worsening pandemic would also affect regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: tourism exports and Chinese tourists In the short term, the outbreak will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Judging from the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these effects may be temporary, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and geographical spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although corporate earnings are expected by the market to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged the search for yield, thereby pushing up asset prices without support from fundamentals. As a result, regional equity markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituent stocks of benchmark equity indices Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for the region’s private sector to service its debt. Although lower domestic interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector may also intensify as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, although this effect may be confined to financially sounder firms and their long-term borrowing. Third, in terms of external factors, East Asian economies may face increased risks from increasingly protectionist US trade policies. Despite recent progress on the China-US Phase One trade agreement, trade tensions between the two countries persist because fundamental trade issues remain unresolved. As evidenced by the widening trade surpluses with the US among several regional economies (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek additional sourcing channels outside China-centred supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging market economies, excluding China, with the US had risen to approximately US$167 billion. If trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the Asian economies concerned may become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed punitive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surplus with the US Over the past decade, increasing integration of international financial markets has led to significant growth in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices, commonly known as passive funds, but also actively managed funds that use investment indices as references.9 By bringing in overseas investors that the economies concerned would otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Such funds therefore enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor bases, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of their markets. But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are market concerns that investment by such funds may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby leading to high corporate leverage.10 In addition, it has been argued that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has increased the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, even more vulnerable.11 This box assesses the financial stability implications of index-driven investment in relation to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to constituent bonds according to each bond’s weight in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave issuers of index constituent bonds with little incentive to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, creating significant credit and debt-servicing risks for the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of firms in individual emerging market economies in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of passive bond fund investment in their bonds,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term, rather than short-term, leverage ratios of the corporate issuers concerned. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated effects. In addition to promoting the development of emerging market corporate bond markets, the broader long-term bond investor base resulting from passive bond funds also benefits the development of emerging market firms. We also find that the above effects are significant only for emerging market firms with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with greater debt-servicing capacity and lower leverage ratios (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged firms or those with weaker debt-servicing capacity do not appear to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. Overall, the above findings suggest that growth in passive bond fund investment may not substantially increase debt-servicing risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending and poor export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, while the recent coronavirus outbreak has also brought substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. In year-on-year terms, real gross domestic product contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis. Chart 3.1 Real gross domestic product growth and contributions from major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real gross domestic product fell successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main drag on gross domestic product in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, and private consumption therefore contracted markedly from the third quarter onwards. 33 Amid heightened economic uncertainties and worsening business sentiment, gross investment spending remained weak and dragged down gross domestic product in the fourth quarter. 34 On the external front, amid escalating China-US trade tensions, weakening global economic growth and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued (Chart 3.2). 35 Affected by the sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down gross domestic product in the third quarter but supported gross domestic product growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Given the strong headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to ease the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment and support enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and sectors that had been severely affected, such as retail, food services, transport and tourism. 36 To give banks greater scope to step up support for the local economy and help moderate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong’s economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, while the recent outbreak has also brought substantial downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, the series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget could provide assistance to households and enterprises, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to enterprises with a 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 The HKMA’s further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks greater scope to step up support for the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressures as a result of the outbreak. Analysed by gross domestic product component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak because of fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the near term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). In particular, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year on year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly attributable to the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year on year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Box 3 examines recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook in greater detail. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build through the third quarter of 2019, mainly because of rising fresh pork prices; as economic activity subsequently weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed. In year-on-year terms, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the rate of increase eased slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was attributable to reduced price pressures across a number of Consumer Price Index components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained notable because of rising fresh pork prices, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. For services, as growth in newly contracted private residential rents slowed earlier, growth in the rental component of the Consumer Price Index also trended downwards (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures increased slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to moderate, the housing rent component of inflation should ease further. On the external front, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation of between 0.6% and 3.7% in 2020, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation of 2.5% and headline inflation of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe than expected economic deterioration, for example because of a prolonged coronavirus outbreak, could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, more severe disruptions to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this background, this box analyses recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook, including why the overall labour market remained broadly resilient during the first three quarters of 2019, with the unemployment rate almost unchanged, and what implications this has for future developments. It also examines some risk factors that could cause the unemployment rate to rise sharply. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real gross domestic product by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature may explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real gross domestic product growth and unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt severe blows to employment in the trade sector and the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors continued to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financing, business services, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, while financial activities relating to fintech development and initial public offerings were also very active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financing and business services sectors. In addition, public administration, social and personal services, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real gross domestic product, public administration, social and personal services respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even when the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against an increase in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment during the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted markedly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment declined during the economic recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some changes in the structure of the labour market also warrant attention. In particular, the increasing proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the shares of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment have declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (around 7% in 2017). 42 Companies may therefore be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours at present, partly reflecting the larger number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with its upward momentum increasing further in December and keeping the exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was attributable partly to equity-related demand and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards the year end. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. Although the coronavirus outbreak may trigger market sentiment and lead to greater volatility in fund flows amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding capital outflow pressures without compromising local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar increased further, and from mid-December to February the exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was attributable partly to buoyant initial public offering activity and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards the year end. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had only a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, movements in the real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked those in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates In measuring fund flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinctly different but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the monetary dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong’s banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong’s financial system as a whole. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. In monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, causing the exchange rate to weaken. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA will stand ready to buy Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, and the Aggregate Balance will consequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, while the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. Therefore, no significant outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits in Hong Kong’s banking system are a useful indicator. When substantial funds flow out of Hong Kong’s banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no significant cross-border fund outflows. Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly, indicating that the coronavirus outbreak had so far had only a limited impact on local monetary conditions. Nevertheless, the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak need to be closely monitored. With ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. Despite uncertainty in the external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained large, increasing by 4.0% from end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As neither Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the monetary base During the review period, broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and then edged up by 0.2% over the seven months since end-June 2019. A counterpart asset analysis indicates that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since end-June mainly reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and an expansion of the monetary base, driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). Over the seven months since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits, the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Over the seven months since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions have grown steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s total broad money supply also rose at a relatively steady pace, with total M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5%, respectively, since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand and business- and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2) Although monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, as initial public offering activity in Hong Kong’s stock market became more active, the overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced greater volatility in late October and around mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally rose. Subscriptions for large initial public offerings exert significant pressure on the overnight rate. The empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to future initial public offering activity also affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. This occurs when market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large initial public offerings and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downward in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on three-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average interest rate on new mortgages At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. The increase mainly reflected banks’ continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, which resulted in a rise in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of October 2019, several retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, retail banks’ best lending rates currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans benchmarked against the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate, major banks raised the interest rate cap determined by reference to the best lending rate, causing the average interest rate on new mortgages to rise to around 2.63% in October. 45 As best lending rates in the market were lowered from November onwards, the average mortgage rate subsequently edged down to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates track movements in US dollar interest rates over the longer term, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates may be affected by local factors that influence demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as initial public offering activity in Hong Kong. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funds. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. If short-term liquidity becomes tight, banks may make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid the possibility of escalating China-US trade tensions, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations that China and the United States would resume trade negotiations reversed the renminbi’s depreciation trend. Both the offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly appreciated beyond 6.9 in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States. However, since the end of January, both the offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced depreciation pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, but generally traded at a premium later in 2019. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, although the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to MSCI’s A-share adjustments, and again at the end of January 2020 around the Lunar New Year holiday.

Amid increasing uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined slightly in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although growth in total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it continued to outpace deposit growth during the review period. Accordingly, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio and Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions increased. However, given the stable level of the Aggregate Balance of the banking system and broadly steady deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit59 of retail banks declined slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, from 1.23% in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses resulted in a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three 25-basis-point reductions in the US federal funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has so far not experienced significant downward pressure. Instead, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, driven by a number of local factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market. Meanwhile, longer-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (the blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term, stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained low by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in the US dollar funding costs of locally licensed banks offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of locally licensed banks edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates, supporting banking-sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. Overall funding costs and maturities have therefore been calculated as weighted averages of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Accordingly, figures from June 2019 onward are not directly comparable with those for earlier months. Looking ahead, a number of downside risks in the external and domestic environments will continue to cloud the earnings outlook for banks. These include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of China-US trade relations and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could undermine already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, potentially putting pressure on banks’ future net interest margins. Domestically, the local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to dampen business investment and market confidence. Against an already weak economic backdrop, if the situation persists or deteriorates further, the outlook for credit demand and banks’ asset quality could worsen. In terms of overall market development, following the granting of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector began launching virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market shares by attracting new customers through more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate because virtual banks’ current scale of operations is still limited, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate their adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results of Box 5 show that the extent of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically associated with improvements in cost efficiency and higher profitability. The capitalization of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above minimum international standards. At the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, the Basel III non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement serves to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions As measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio65 requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions increased from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Category 1 institutions remained high at 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions remained high at 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and robust funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding a variety of liquidity shocks. At the end of 2019, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Overall, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions increased from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the year. Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system had remained stable since April 2019 and deposits were broadly steady, there were no clear signs of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. It was estimated that, under a hypothetical shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). On a half-yearly basis, loan growth, as measured by changes in the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions, increased moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019 before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was attributable to slower growth during the review period in both domestic loans, including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively, in the second half of 2019, lower than the respective increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half.
