The rollout of coronavirus disease (COVID-19) vaccines has brought hope of economic reopening and boosted the global growth outlook. Together with continued fiscal and monetary accommodation, this has propelled financial markets to successive record highs. Nevertheless, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the lasting economic scars caused by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level against the US dollar, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant fund outflows from the local banking system. Partly reflecting subdued economic activity and lower credit demand amid recurrent waves of the pandemic, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, although a modest increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant to the impact of the associated downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again from the fourth quarter amid a resurgence in COVID-19 infections. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development towards the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, facilitating a return of the global economy to normality and an acceleration in growth. Together with continued fiscal and monetary accommodation, this pushed global financial markets to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this background, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be widely distributed. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive policy accommodation may result in higher-than-expected inflation, which could in turn prompt central banks to scale back monetary accommodation earlier than expected, bringing an end to financial markets’ expectations of a “lower-for-longer” monetary policy stance. Over the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio inflows into the region rebounded and the search for yield re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia continues to face persistent pandemic-related uncertainties. First, amid global competition for vaccine procurement, the region’s less-developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hampering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage or effectiveness, together with weakening fiscal positions among governments in the region, may dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activity gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will continue to depend heavily on developments in the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. After depreciating for several months at the beginning of 2020, the renminbi strengthened over the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened and the Mainland bond market recorded strong capital inflows. A detailed study shows that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Box 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level. As domestic demand edged up and goods exports expanded further, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first consecutive annual declines in history. The latest sectoral GDP data show that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely than the overall economy during the pandemic. In response to the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two more rounds—the third and fourth rounds—of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong’s capability to combat it. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including the distribution of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of 100%-guaranteed personal concessionary loans to unemployed persons. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, as well as an extension of the repayment period for trade facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines offering hope that economic activity can return to normal, the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole, but the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including developments in the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% in 2021, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, its highest level since the SARS outbreak. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government introduced the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell markedly year on year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and declined further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, an indicator of inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to stay modest in the near term. In particular, slower growth in newly contracted private residential rents earlier will continue to restrain local inflation. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying and headline inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level against the US dollar, driven mainly by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering activities and Southbound inflows through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fund-raising activity remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. An analysis by geographical location shows that total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant fund outflows from the local banking system. Although uncertainties associated with the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may heighten capital-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system and is therefore capable of withstanding such volatility. As the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. As funding costs declined, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Alongside the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with the premium averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, renminbi bank lending in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased, and the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level of RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has an efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-boundary channels for capital flows linking to the Mainland. As the Mainland continues to open its capital account, international investors’ demand for renminbi assets increases, and regional economic and financial cooperation deepens under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by rising global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through Southbound Stock Connect, the local stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global stock markets rose because of factors including unprecedented monetary easing by major economies; optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery in economic activity; and reduced global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses following a sharp decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and at one point surpassing the 31,000 level in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded as market confidence recovered rapidly in response to unprecedented economic stimulus measures introduced by governments worldwide. Although bond yields rebounded moderately over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, continued to hover near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expected the COVID-19 pandemic eventually to come to an end and global economic growth to accelerate thereafter. Together with expectations of a global “lower for longer” monetary policy stance, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, financial markets’ buoyant expectations were disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment, and asset prices could become volatile if the economic recovery proved weaker than expected or policy support was withdrawn earlier than anticipated, for example because inflation exceeded expectations. Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support and how to address the many problems left by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and lasting economic scarring. Persistent pandemic-related uncertainty continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, where less-developed emerging market economies may face greater challenges in procuring and distributing vaccines. Any setbacks in vaccination programmes could reverse the prevailing optimism and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activity gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remains highly uncertain and will depend largely on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The Government therefore announced that it would maintain its supportive policy stance while emphasising the importance of containing systemic risks. Benefiting from the release of purchasing power following the reopening of economies, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infections have risen again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social-distancing measures and causing global growth momentum to weaken once more. At the end of 2020, more transmissible variants emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use at the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end and the global economy would return to normal and grow more rapidly. Another force supporting the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus, including major central banks’ commitment to “lower for longer” monetary policies amid subdued inflation and continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021 the International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and the share prices of cyclical sectors that typically benefit from an economic recovery rose, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic environment remained challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control depends on whether vaccines can be distributed widely, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX promote more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supplies are expected to make the problem of low vaccination rates more severe in lower-income emerging market economies. If the pandemic is not brought under control as hoped, social-distancing and other restrictive measures may need to be extended, thereby undermining the outlook for the global recovery. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population having received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets was founded on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the “lower for longer” monetary policy stance. However, there is a risk that support measures will be withdrawn more quickly than expected. For example, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary accommodation, while higher-than-expected inflation data could also increase volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 US and euro-area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, there is significant uncertainty about future China-US relations. The wave of China-US “decoupling”, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance towards Mainland China among both Democrats and Republicans in the United States, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. Although withdrawing such measures prematurely could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a “cliff effect”, these measures are costly in the long run, including the fiscal burden they impose and the delays they cause to the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources, for example by allowing “zombie companies” with no longer viable business models to survive through continued government support. In addition, policymakers must address the many problems left by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 because of declining corporate revenues and surging government expenditure (Chart 2.5). Although the problems arising from the sharp increase in debt may not be imminent because global interest rates are currently extremely low, continued debt accumulation in the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy issue concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty may cause companies to reduce investment, while workers suffering from prolonged unemployment may permanently leave the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after plunging in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was driven mainly by a rebound in exports, with demand particularly strong for exports of electronics and technology equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers, remained under strain. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite continued uncertainty surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment flows resumed. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted increased bond inflows because of improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were launched, equity inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly amid portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by around 10% from its low in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows East Asia continues to face persistent pandemic-related uncertainty. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the region’s hard-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early vaccine supplies has raised procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region’s logistics and public-health capacity. As a result, less-developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, while uneven vaccination across economies may prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism has been driven largely by the vaccine rollout, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations. An abrupt decline in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. As COVID-19 was successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovered, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports continued to grow, supported by strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-technology products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, Mainland GDP still grew by 2.3% despite the unprecedented shock to the economy caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions of demand components to GDP growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained will still depend to some extent on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activity in the Mainland has normalised, the service sector remains partly disrupted following renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. As regards the external environment, although export growth resumed in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain because of new waves of the pandemic in most developed economies. In addition, China-US tensions may not ease in the short term, although the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the agreed Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the European Union will help further integrate China with other economies and may partly offset the adverse effects of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Given the continued uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, the Government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that there would be no major change to the existing policy stance in 2021 in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of containing systemic risks, such as maintaining stable macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identifies self-reliance and strength in science and technology and the dual-circulation strategy as development priorities, with the aim of raising per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on bond issuers’ repayment capacity appeared limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, the total value of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 because of a sharp rise in defaults on state-owned enterprise bonds (Chart 2.9). Although the increase in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflected the Central Government’s determination to break the “rigid repayment” convention for state-owned enterprises in order to promote more rational market pricing of risk, constrained fiscal space among some local governments, particularly those in less-developed regions, may also have been a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Amount and ratio of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to higher financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: Five-year corporate bond yields In the property market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By comparison, housing prices in lower-tier cities rose much more slowly (Chart 2.11). The excess housing supply that had troubled third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below its peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real gross domestic product (GDP) remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 amid a recovery in domestic demand and further expansion in goods exports. With hopes that COVID-19 vaccination would enable economic activity to return to normal, the Hong Kong economy was expected to resume growth in 2021 after recording its sharpest contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to considerable uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine roll-outs. As widespread vaccination would take time, the Hong Kong economy would continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. The labour market was therefore expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures would remain mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below its pre-pandemic level. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first consecutive annual declines ever recorded. The latest data on GDP by economic activity also showed that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with contractions in consumption- and tourism-related sectors more severe than that in the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover in the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters. However, consumer confidence remained weak as the authorities reimposed social-distancing measures amid the third and fourth local waves of the pandemic. Overall investment expenditure also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment temporarily improved. Hong Kong’s trade in goods expanded further, partly benefiting from stronger export performance, particularly exports to Mainland China (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism was still at a standstill. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting the slower recovery in goods exports than in imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions from major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports In response to the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund, totalling HK$30.4 billion, between September and December 2020 to assist sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong’s anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including the distribution of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal concessionary loans to unemployed persons. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced a further extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines offering hope that economic activity could return to normal, the Hong Kong economy was expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to considerable uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine roll-outs. As widespread vaccination would take time, the domestic economy would continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, which would in turn affect Hong Kong’s trade in goods and inbound tourism. The Government forecast real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, the highest level in 17 years (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, its highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while government figures showed a continued decline in job vacancies. The year-on-year growth of the nominal index of payroll per person engaged, a measure of labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the domestic labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation declined markedly year on year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, a measure of inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. Specifically, price pressures on basic food eased, while the cost of meals bought away from home declined visibly, reflecting the take-away discounts offered by more restaurants while dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other tradable goods, such as durable goods, remained moderate. On the services front, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained weak as private residential rents consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs As global and domestic economic conditions remained challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong were expected to remain mild in the near term. In particular, domestic inflation would continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly contracted private residential rents. The market consensus forecast headline inflation at a moderate 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecast underlying inflation of 1% and headline inflation of 1.6% for 2021. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism rapidly fell into a slump, raising market concerns that the crisis might have scarring effects on the subsequent labour market recovery. Against this background, this box empirically analyses the impact of a tourism boom on Hong Kong’s labour market to explore the potential implications of the current tourism slump. Inbound tourism has experienced dramatic ups and downs since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Visitor arrivals began to surge after the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply as individuals to visit Hong Kong once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry IVS endorsements permitting multiple visits to Hong Kong within one year. The number of Mainland visitors subsequently increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure links with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached an all-time high between late 2018 and early 2019. The local social incidents that followed halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, while inbound tourism had been at a standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies We use the tourism boom generated by the IVS as an example to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We regard the introduction of the IVS in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock because its timing was largely exogenous and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. The main data for our analysis are population data from Hong Kong’s Population Censuses or By-censuses. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. We also define tourism-related sectors as the food and beverage services, retail, hotel and transport sectors. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences analytical framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers aged 20–40 in the treatment group and older workers aged 41–65 in the comparison group. We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because, being at an earlier stage of their careers, they could make major changes to their employment choices more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the labour market impact of the tourism boom generated by the IVS could change over time, we also use an event study to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers, particularly women and workers with only secondary education, were more likely to enter tourism-related sectors after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the effect of the IVS on the probability of young women working in tourism-related sectors was especially significant and persistent, remaining close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards, in terms of the average difference from the older cohort in the probability of entering such sectors (Chart B2.2). Using a similar approach, we also compare the income of workers in tourism-related sectors, the treatment group, with that of workers in non-tourism-related sectors, the comparison group. The estimates show that, after the implementation of the IVS, income growth among workers in tourism-related sectors was higher than among employees in non-tourism-related sectors. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other sectors, female workers and less-educated workers employed in tourism-related sectors recorded larger and increasing income gains of 3–20 percentage points (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on the income of women and less-educated workers The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and less-educated workers. In Hong Kong’s case, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses showing that strong growth in inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism has fallen from boom to trough, these groups of workers may be more severely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, and the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times during September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities and southbound fund flows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates declined across the board. Although uncertainties associated with developments in the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and continued China-US tensions may exacerbate volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and is capable of withstanding pressures arising from volatile fund flows. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund flows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some IPO proceeds were remitted out of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505–7.7544 in November and December amid improved sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards the year end. With fundraising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the Aggregate Balance increased as the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, reflecting substantial inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. In September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of substantial fund outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual fund movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar declined, broadly tracking the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had only a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, movements in the real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked those in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties associated with developments in the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and continued China-US tensions may exacerbate volatility in fund flows. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities, such as IPOs, which result in substantial fund inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, these fundraising activities may attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, and is capable of withstanding volatility in fund flows without compromising financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, local monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the repeated triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. Other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities increased Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, resulting in significant increases in Hong Kong dollar broad money (HK$M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component from July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, HK$M3 increased sharply again, mainly driven by a large-scale IPO at the end of January. Overall, HK$M3 grew by 21.7% over the seven months since the end of June; excluding the effect of the IPO at the end of January, HK$M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. According to an analysis of counterpart assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HK$M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the Monetary Base resulting from the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As the major component of HK$M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the effect of the IPO at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined because of low deposit rates, the decline was more than fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in HK$M3 and counterpart assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting US dollar weakness, while deposits in other foreign currencies grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions rose sharply by 13.2% during the review period owing to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate because of various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand and business- and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. As the Aggregate Balance increased, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates did not fluctuate significantly because of ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked movements in the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on three-year Hong Kong Government Bonds edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on ten-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points over the same period to 1.30%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, the Composite Interest Rate and the average lending rate for new mortgages Retail Hong Kong dollar interest rates generally declined in tandem with Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates. The Composite Interest Rate, which reflects the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, declined further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). As funding costs decreased, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking movements in the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low level of US interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations arising from capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the more favourable economic outlook in Mainland China compared with the rest of the world, as well as US dollar weakness. FTSE Russell’s announcement at the end of September that Mainland government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index provided further investment-demand support for the renminbi’s appreciation. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with the premium averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced brief fluctuations owing to occasional demand for northbound remittances and seasonal liquidity demand towards the year end, it remained below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). The three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate declined in late December in tandem with onshore renminbi interest rates, before rising again in late January, partly owing to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Fixings of overnight and three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow. Since the fourth quarter, growth in renminbi deposits accelerated, reflecting to some extent the appreciation of the renminbi and its higher interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, increasing by 21.9% to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021 (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of this amount, renminbi customer deposits increased by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi businesses, outstanding renminbi loans declined by 2.4% over the seven months since the end of June 2020 to RMB159.2 billion. Meanwhile, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, representing year-on-year growth of 16.7%. Among these transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland grew faster than remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a sizeable renminbi liquidity pool sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. In 2020, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

As the recurring COVID-19 pandemic prolonged the economic downturn, compounded by the impact of the persistently low interest rate environment, the profitability of Hong Kong’s retail banks declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, Hong Kong’s banking sector remained sound, underpinned by its continued strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic could be brought under control and economic activity could resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions will weigh on business activity and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic will impair the repayment capacity of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the related downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit fell by 38.5% from the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). Retail banks’ net interest margin narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the corresponding period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that outweighed the modest increase in non-interest income and thereby reduced profitability. For 2020 as a whole, retail banks’ aggregate pre-tax operating profit fell by 29.4%, while return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profitability Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margin Largely driven by substantial fund inflows arising from stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate, a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, followed a broadly similar trend, falling markedly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of locally licensed banks fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks’ net interest margins. In addition, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have strengthened market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the banking sector’s loan quality and profitability in the near term. The capital position of Hong Kong’s banking sector remained sound and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions was 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated that authorized institutions’ funding positions were stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained high at 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. Authorized institutions’ ample liquidity and sound funding positions indicated that Hong Kong’s banking sector was capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system’s stable funding structure. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions As the total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans declined during the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, at the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratios declined to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, from 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposures of locally incorporated licensed banks remained relatively low in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a prolonged economic downturn caused by the recurring pandemic and tighter social-distancing measures, total loans and advances declined moderately in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, total credit in the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although the pace of growth slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, after increasing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions decreased by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans, comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, after growing by 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, after declining by 2.0% in the first half of the year, Hong Kong dollar loans at the end of 2020 remained broadly at a level similar to that at the end of June. After rising sharply by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, foreign currency loans decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector became slightly more optimistic about the short-term outlook for credit demand than six months earlier. The HKMA’s December 2020 Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that the proportion of respondent authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decline over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment capacity of households and corporates, banks’ loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance remained weak, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks and the possibility that monetary policy tightening may be more aggressive than expected if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. If the Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy substantially and thereby causes global financial conditions to tighten, the recoveries of more vulnerable emerging market economies will come under pressure. More recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have significant repercussions for the global economy through trade and financial channels and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, growth in total bank lending accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the continued economic recovery, while the potentially faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation will also pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness extending into 2022, as the spread of the highly transmissible Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on mobility worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. More recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices may further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may result in an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainty. In the short term, large-scale pandemic outbreaks could lead to the reimposition of lockdown measures and a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected has increased, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating its timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions may also tighten, impairing borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recoveries of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. More recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, aggravate shortages in the supply of industrial goods, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the renewed imposition of stringent anti-pandemic measures in some Southeast Asian economies in the third quarter temporarily slowed the recovery momentum, while the region’s technology-product-exporting economies, namely South Korea and Singapore, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and constrained public healthcare resources. Second, faster policy normalisation by the Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures, making the trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity more difficult for regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery. Third, slower growth in major economies, coupled with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, increases in the prices of various commodities triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will feed through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Together with heightened uncertainty in the global economy, this will further complicate regional central banks’ monetary policy normalisation decisions. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the longer term, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors will need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risks and how such sensitivity is affected by firms’ environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term because of the prolonged property market downturn and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. The Mainland authorities have therefore made stabilising growth their top priority this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Both total onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises decreased in the second half of 2021, and Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risks to the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks, particularly systemically important banks, have limited exposure to loans to property developers, as well as low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew moderately, as merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the continued global economic recovery, improving local labour market conditions and the Government’s launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022–23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and their application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking industry, has also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong’s economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, although growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the continuing pandemic and a higher base effect. In particular, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to a number of uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures were re-emerging amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tighter anti-pandemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets generally higher in the final quarter of 2021, propelling the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. Owing to the rapid global spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and broadened to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy stance, increasing the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations and adversely affect emerging markets, where recoveries generally continued to lag. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant across the region, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with the region’s major technology-exporting economies continuing to outperform other economies. Although the Omicron variant is currently unlikely to seriously derail the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cloud the region’s economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy could trigger asset price corrections in the region, while slower growth in major economies could weigh on the region’s merchandise export growth. On the one hand, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has raised commodity prices and increased inflation risks; on the other hand, it will weaken consumption and heighten global economic uncertainty, making monetary policy normalisation decisions more complicated for central banks in the region. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of coronavirus infections, power restrictions and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from the cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the Government has made stabilising growth its top priority for the year, and macroeconomic policies will also provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the spread of the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with that of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply chain problems, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global gross domestic product growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China, which offset the expected rebound in growth elsewhere in Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF forecasts of real gross domestic product growth While global economic growth slowed, inflationary pressures continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, rose markedly in major advanced economies, particularly the United States, which had implemented policy stimulus on a larger scale since the onset of the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures broadened to a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up the prices of various commodities and may exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures.
