(2) “Advanced Asian economies” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) “Emerging Asian market economies” include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainty and tilted towards the downside, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment unfolds, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far responded to the recent surge in Omicron cases with targeted measures focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less stringent measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown tentative signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should a large-scale outbreak occur, the reimposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could in turn cause supply bottlenecks to worsen again. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index—supplier delivery times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief from goods inflation. However, several developments could cause the current high level of global inflation to persist for longer than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imported from Russia will push up commodity prices, higher production costs being passed through to final selling prices with a lag, earlier sharp increases in global residential property prices driving up rents in the future, tight labour markets posing upside risks to wage growth, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, no longer characterising high inflation as “transitory”, doubling the pace of asset purchase reductions from US$15 billion to US$30 billion per month with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing indicated that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates multiple times during 2022. By contrast, given the euro area’s closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this background, and with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated following a prolonged period of accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures require the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity could be at risk of deterioration and financial market volatility could be triggered. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe escalated, risk aversion in financial markets increased and signs of US dollar shortages emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Amid a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce these funds’ liquidity risks during periods of market stress, and examines the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as major technology-exporting economies in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the unevenness of the recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures remained moderate in several emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index Emerging Asian markets are widely expected to experience a broad-based recovery in 2022, but the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread across the region since the end of 2021, its economic impact has remained milder than that of previous waves of infections. However, some regional economies where vaccination rates still lag and public health resources are relatively constrained will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy could trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support their economic recoveries will face more difficult trade-offs between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, given the historically high correlation between the two (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in US long-term yields could also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, heightening the risk of corrections in the region’s asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian ten-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the outlook for the region’s merchandise trade faces uncertainties arising from slowdowns in major economies and the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which could weaken the region’s export growth. Chart 2.6 United States: imports from emerging Asia and real gross domestic product Fourth, although the region’s economies have relatively limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, commodity price increases triggered by the conflict will feed through to inflation in the region while weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, this will make monetary policy normalisation decisions more complicated for central banks in the region. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted the region’s economies to the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to attach greater importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms’ environmental performance. The coronavirus pandemic caused a severe shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Outflows from selected open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another reason for the substantial outflows may have been that investors exercised a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming their fund holdings early, thereby avoiding redemption costs that could rise sharply under market stress. To curb outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing—an open-ended fund pricing rule that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, no empirical research has established whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this background, this box conducts an empirical study to determine whether swing pricing reduced outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. In addition, this box seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we put forward policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming before other investors, thereby passing redemption costs on to them. First-mover advantage exists mainly in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs incurred by a fund’s investors, such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments, are reflected in the open-ended fund’s price after the transactions are executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear such transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, especially when substantial redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced because redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

Supported by continued growth in goods exports and private consumption, the Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, recording positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on domestic economic activity. The overall economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the recovery will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the near term alongside higher import prices, weak domestic rents and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. In year-on-year terms, real gross domestic product grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth slowed from the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real gross domestic product grew by 6.4%, the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real gross domestic product growth and contributions from major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). On the domestic front, improving labour market conditions, coupled with the Government’s Consumption Voucher Scheme, boosted private consumption. However, overall investment spending declined in the final quarter following strong rebounds in the preceding two consecutive quarters. On the external front, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remained robust amid the continued recovery of the global economy, while trade in services remained weak, partly because inbound tourism was still at a standstill (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade dragged on gross domestic product in the third quarter but supported gross domestic product growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volumes A new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on domestic economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year option to make partial principal repayments, which is also available for loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the continuing pandemic and a higher base effect. In particular, Hong Kong’s goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent pandemic developments, the faster pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns, such as the Russia-Ukraine situation, have clouded the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could stimulate domestic economic growth. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, although it remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures had re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected fewer new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and tighter anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on local pandemic developments and the pace of the domestic economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures have broadly increased in recent months, but remain moderate. In year-on-year terms, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. In particular, as domestic demand recovered and external prices rose (Chart 3.5), prices of meals bought away from home and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained weak, they rose slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average salaries (Chart 3.7). However, weak rents and moderate domestic labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast is for the headline inflation rate to reach 2.4% in 2022, while the Government forecasts a headline inflation rate of 2.1% and an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for 2022.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened during the review period amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over US monetary policy normalisation. With ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may intensify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand shocks arising from volatile fund flows. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone most of the time, with trading continuing to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly because of weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. Initial public offering fundraising activities continued to support the Hong Kong dollar during the review period (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of fund outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of unusual cross-border fund flows. Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. As US dollar interest rates rise, outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds—the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions—may cause the Hong Kong dollar to weaken and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in accordance with the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Hong Kong also has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand fund flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 1.4% in the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuances to meet banks’ continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample banking system liquidity, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion during the review period to HK$1,188.7 billion, with the Aggregate Balance before Discount Window activities decreasing correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). It is therefore appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. With ample banking system liquidity, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low despite market concerns over US monetary policy tightening (Chart 4.7). On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample banking system liquidity can provide an adequate buffer during large-scale capital market activities or periods of financial market volatility. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand near year-end, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate showed slight volatility in late December 2021, while the three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Major global stock markets continued to advance in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated from January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to help mitigate its impacts. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted considerable effort to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 as a standalone report for the first time this year. I hope this report will provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong’s banking system to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA’s major functions. Readers will learn about our specific measures and initiatives in this report, with the following key highlights: Banks’ day-to-day operations are exposed to climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks’ climate resilience. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and explored how technology could be harnessed to help banks assess the impacts of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we also shared with the industry sound practices for the proper management of these products, with a view to strengthening banks’ climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives to address climate risks and promote the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework. The framework will enhance financial market transparency and promote greater alignment among green finance policies. Internationally, we actively participate in a number of international organisations, contributing to the formulation of policies to address climate change and the assessment of its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a very challenging year for global bond markets, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth, rising by 42% to a total of US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong Asia’s largest centre for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the Hainan Provincial People’s Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing nearly US$16 billion worth of green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects covering areas such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two “firsts”. In May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural batch of government green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion, which was the world’s largest green retail bond issuance at the time. We also assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural tokenised green bond in February 2023. It was the world’s first tokenised green bond issued by a government, and the issuance marked a significant milestone in successfully combining our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and can only be established through the efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works primarily through the Steering Group with relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to developing a local green classification framework as mentioned above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training within the industry and improves Hong Kong’s data resources through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance. The Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas, including mandatory climate-related disclosures and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, notably by setting a target of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced our risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capture the potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment by the Exchange Fund and identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the portfolio’s long-term returns. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had fallen by 43% from its 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to carbon-intensive assets has remained lower than that of the overall market. Going forward, we will continue to progress towards our net-zero target by further integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, exercising active ownership, maintaining ongoing collaboration with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: the environment, our people and social responsibility. On the environmental front, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and fostering a more environmentally friendly market for the community. On the people front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively cultivate a healthy and inclusive work environment. On the social responsibility front, we are committed to enhancing financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion and giving back to the community. Compared with the levels recorded when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption all achieved double-digit reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the near term, our target is to eliminate Scope 1 emissions completely and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this critical global issue, we recognise that we must take action ourselves, lead by example, and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s near-term plans and priorities for addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in pursuing this goal. We are confident that, through the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the wider community, we can successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong’s financial sector and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development of, and best practices in, green and sustainable finance. As the banking regulator, we will work to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate considerations into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector’s “Green and Sustainable Banking Baseline”. The HKMA will also support banks’ efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, including by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, quantify and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regular regulator-led stress-testing exercise for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to withstand climate risks under an enhanced stress-testing framework covering various stress scenarios, including extreme weather events and adverse economic conditions. To foster the sound development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will closely monitor local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to further develop the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector’s green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green taxonomy framework. On market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in increasing the issuance of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the Programme’s scope to cover sustainability bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA is also assisting in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. We will also continue to collaborate with other authorities and government departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will jointly launch various dedicated initiatives in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market insights, offering banks targeted professional training, and providing practical guidance to help banks formulate roadmaps for developing green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme and expand its influence across Asia. The Alliance will also step up efforts to enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate the sharing of green finance knowledge, and spearhead programmes in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to contributing to global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management processes, work towards its net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares about its staff, the wider community and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to contributing to global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon emissions reduction and encourage staff to lend their full support by conserving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide staff with further guidance on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To advance digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications, further improve operational efficiency, and minimise, as far as possible, the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been working to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to the impacts of various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has placed particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their ability to detect environmental crime and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crime and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how such risks are addressed under the existing Basel Framework. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1, “Climate Risk Management”, in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress and challenges regarding the implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process and communicated it to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1, “Risk-based Supervisory Approach”, and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, drawing on experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA also formulated plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular regulator-led stress-testing exercise, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. In view of the growing prevalence of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. During the thematic reviews, the HKMA identified a number of sound practices and shared them with the industry through a circular issued in December, enabling banks to progressively enhance their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks’ capacity to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions could facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices; this work employs advanced analytics and regulatory technology, complemented by fully automated supervisory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the collection of anti-money laundering supervisory data to reduce banks’ manual workload and paper consumption. To enhance transparency across financial markets and improve the consistency of green finance policies, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. A green classification framework, commonly known as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable and provides a reference for authorities and market participants in determining whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore the framework’s features and challenges in depth, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the framework’s structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognising the potential risks that climate change may pose to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its existing surveillance work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On the research front, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022 to examine two major topics in depth: greenwashing in the corporate green bond market3 and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposure4. The findings of these studies help inform the formulation of policies and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and its Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s Liquidity Facilities Framework is a secured standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is exploring the incorporation of sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps promote international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, while drawing insights from these discussions to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA stepped up its efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives in alignment with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government’s climate strategies1. The Steering Group’s work is mainly guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out six key long-term focus areas and five near-term action points to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem for a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre Promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection Enhance relevant skills among practitioners and raise public awareness and understanding Encourage product innovation and research initiatives to channel capital towards green and sustainable projects Capitalise on opportunities presented by the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) Strengthen regional and international collaboration Actions taken to date to advance sustainable finance development in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Its current priorities include capacity building and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), a green taxonomy (see “Developing a green classification framework to facilitate green financing” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, in March the Steering Group announced the preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong and will support Hong Kong’s development into a regional carbon trading centre, including by developing a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalising on opportunities arising from GBA collaboration. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability and sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of the collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting unlisted companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which facilitates corporate sustainability reporting and helps financial institutions collect and analyse company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks an important step in expanding the coverage of the Steering Group’s data work to include SMEs, an important segment of the economy that was previously more difficult to reach. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the work of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions on capacity building and policy development, and to develop resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories on data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, helping the financial sector and other sectors access data and learning resources relating to green and sustainable finance. The repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong To support industry talent development, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other capacity-building initiatives included launching the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new Green and Sustainable Finance module3 under the HKMA’s Enhanced Competency Framework for banking practitioners. Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks4, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions and innovative technology providers to develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to realise their full potential in making green finance a mainstream core business, and to promote the financial system’s participation in global climate change-related activities. How it works Provide financial institutions with a one-stop peer-learning platform to access the knowledge, tools and information needed to formulate their own green finance road maps and transform into credible green financial institutions Bring together green finance leaders and connect green financial institutions across different emerging markets Facilitate dialogue and explore frontier topics Advance the global green finance agenda and unlock boundless green and climate-related investment opportunities In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became cornerstone members of the Alliance and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities, thereby supporting the transition to a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone members, International Finance Corporation and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has held a total of 18 training events and roundtable discussions, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022, the Alliance and the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7 jointly published their first frontier topic research report, entitled “Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulatory Oversight”. The HKMA continued to promote green and sustainable debt issuance and foster a local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022, including bonds and loans, reached US$80.5 billion, representing growth of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion) To demonstrate the Government’s determination to combat climate change, promote green finance, and develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in implementing the related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued close to US$16 billion equivalent in institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the Programme’s transparency and accountability arrangements, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable members of the public to participate in and share the benefits of Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment, the inaugural green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion were issued in May and received enthusiastic public support, making them the world’s largest green retail bond issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong and reinforced Hong Kong’s position as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular institutional green bond issuance programme in the 2022/23 financial year and issued US$5.75 billion equivalent in green bonds in January 2023. The triple-currency offering covered US dollars, euros and renminbi, with tenors ranging from two to 30 years, continuing to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The offering was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government’s previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors’ strong confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the size of the renminbi bond issuance to RMB10 billion. The shares taken up by international investors and Mainland investors participating through Southbound Trading under Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong’s status as the premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was among the world’s first tokenised green bonds issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis over a private blockchain network, while subsequent processes, including coupon payments, secondary-market trade settlement and redemption at maturity, were also digitalised. The Government’s experience from this issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association’s report showed that Hong Kong became Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances in 2022, with bonds arranged in Hong Kong totalling US$27.8 billion and accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances US$27.8 billion Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB5 billion of offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also made its inaugural issuance of RMB5 billion in offshore bonds in Hong Kong, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again underscored Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its longstanding position as the region’s premier fundraising platform. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in 2021, and used the Scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers, including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external reviewers, to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The Scheme was well received by the industry. By the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the expenses of pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both types of external review services for issuers of more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan-size threshold for external review cost subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of a proof of concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Hong Kong Centre of the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitised carbon forwards, also known as mitigation outcome interests (MOIs), with a view to enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022 and successfully developed two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitised MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in support of the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, required its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission, and incorporated environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth”, the HKMA believes that due consideration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate the associated risks. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance its responsible investment journey, including by setting a “net-zero emissions by 2050” target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategies to strengthen portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively contributes to building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment and collaborating with international organisations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures concerning the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Financial Stability Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the Exchange Fund’s investments. The foremost guiding principle is that, consistent with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives, the HKMA should give priority to ESG investments where the risk-adjusted long-term returns are comparable to those of other investments. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Sub-Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Sub-Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors progress in ESG integration and the Exchange Fund’s ESG profile through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s various ESG initiatives. The proposals discussed and work progress reviewed at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Oversight and governance structure for responsible investment The dedicated team in the Risk Management and Compliance Division works closely with the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s various investment teams on ESG integration and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investments: Public market investments The Credit, Rules and Compliance Committee, comprising members of the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG profile of the fixed-income portfolios through regular reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, from an ESG perspective, the Risk Management and Compliance Division participates in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Striving for active ownership” under “Risk Management” on page 27 for details). Private market investments The Investment Sub-Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal conducted by the Risk Management and Compliance Division and the private market investment teams. Concrete evidence² continues to show that climate change and its associated risks have significant impacts. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming that the nationally determined contribution targets announced by all jurisdictions are fully implemented, the increase in global temperature by 2100 is still estimated to reach 2.1°C to 2.4°C, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting the rise in global average temperature to below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. If jurisdictions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and market repricing of assets based on anticipated future trends, together with inherent physical risks, will intensify pressure on asset valuations. In view of updated global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA drew on the expertise of an external consultant to further assess the resilience of the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” under a “rapid transition” scenario (Figure 2), in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021. The “rapid transition” scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments combine to drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are abruptly divested to keep the rise in average temperature within 1.5°C by 2100. This scenario is broadly aligned with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The “Investment Portfolio” remains resilient over the medium to long term because a relatively large proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sectoral distribution is crucial. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets may benefit from the transition. Transition risks and asset repricing could adversely affect performance in the short term, particularly that of equity assets. The “Investment Portfolio” as a whole will experience increasing impacts from physical risks that gradually emerge over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Like other modelling approaches, climate scenario analysis has its limitations. The analysis is based on the sectoral distribution of market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level and does not take into account the effects of actively selecting specific securities within a sector. More in-depth research indicates that investments in the “Investment Portfolio” are generally more resilient to transition shocks, or less severely affected by them, than the strategic asset allocation market benchmarks. This result reaffirms that the HKMA’s responsible investment approach, with its focus on tackling climate change, can enhance portfolio resilience. The climate change trajectory remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities presented by climate change. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities related to the climate transition, climate risk mitigation and enhancement of long-term portfolio returns. Building on its positive momentum, the HKMA increased its holdings of green, social and sustainability bonds by a further 50% in 2022. For equity investments, the HKMA invests in an actively managed governance-themed equity portfolio and applies a decarbonisation strategy to its passive equity portfolios by tilting them towards companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with dedicated general partners of the Exchange Fund’s “Long-Term Growth Portfolio” the establishment of a specialised private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Figure 3). Figure 3 Ongoing measures to increase ESG investments The HKMA invests in a pan-African wind farm operator that, in addition to generating clean energy, places strong emphasis on social factors and biodiversity. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from attacking their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vulture species that were already threatened with extinction. Livestock are important assets for local villagers. To help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the animals from natural predators. In addition, the operator employs a bird monitoring team to issue warnings when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left behind by predators, allowing the wind turbines to be shut down to prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win outcome: it safeguards the villagers’ livelihoods while reducing fatal collisions between vultures and wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can create more business opportunities and open up new revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply-chain-related operation. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China specialising in logistics services for cold-chain pharmaceuticals, chemical products and high-end consumer goods. The company faces increasingly stringent ESG operating standards, mainly because its multinational corporate clients require their service providers to meet ambitious decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these requirements, the company engaged an external consultant to help formulate a “Three-year ESG Plan” aimed at reducing its carbon emissions intensity by 50% by 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan delivered significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures earned the company recognition from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing as a “Low-carbon and Green Management Case”. These achievements and accolades have enabled the company to secure substantial business opportunities from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical products sectors that place particular emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its fourth annual ESG workshop, sharing sound ESG practices with nine participating private market institutions, including general partners, limited partners and corporates, and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In public markets, the HKMA urges its trading counterparties, mainly investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr Howard Lee, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivers the opening remarks at the HKMA ESG Workshop 2022 At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in developing industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a PRI-coordinated joint initiative among signatories to develop a standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaire⁵, ⁶ for private equity and venture capital investments, helping private market investors conduct ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in various working groups supporting FCLTGlobal’s research into leading market practices for long-term portfolios and the decarbonisation of private assets, as well as the application of such practices by long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS Guide on Climate-related Disclosure for Central Banks, demonstrating its commitment to adopting sound ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a workstream under the NGFS “Net Zero for Central Banks” workstream and participates in developing sustainable and responsible investment approaches for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars to share insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms Clara Lau, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (centre), speaks at an ESG investment opportunities sharing session Building internal capabilities is essential to continuing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to undertake sustainability-related courses and obtain relevant qualifications, the HKMA has also acquired relevant knowledge and practical experience through the process, initiated in 2021, of engaging an external consultant to advise on leading industry practices for portfolio climate transition. The HKMA also uses ESG data compiled by reputable external information providers to supplement its ongoing portfolio analysis, helping to strengthen the Exchange Fund’s ESG resilience.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own organisational carbon footprint, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier and contributing to Hong Kong’s overall climate goals. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also fulfils its commitments to caring for the physical and mental well-being of its staff, promoting financial inclusion and discharging its social responsibilities. The HKMA is committed to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA puts the concept of sustainability into practice under three pillars: the environment, employees and social responsibility (Diagram 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee is responsible for leading the formulation and implementation of the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives and representatives from the Risk and Compliance Department and the Corporate Development and Services Department, and submits regular reports to the Governance Sub-Committee of the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the Committee’s leadership, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing measures in their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved climate targets for corporate operations and reviewed the transition roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to review progress on the HKMA’s green initiatives, including proposals to strengthen the HKMA’s sustainable procurement policies, procedures and approaches. Sustainability Governance Structure The HKMA’s Corporate Sustainability Journey In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, its employees and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the “15 Years Plus Caring Organisation” logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA attaches great importance to its organisational carbon footprint and has established internal Green Office Guidelines to manage the environmental impact of its operational processes. The HKMA has incorporated environmental considerations into the interior design, operation, repair and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, BEAM Plus awarded the HKMA a Gold rating for certain renovated office areas. This was the second green building certification received, following the LEED Gold certification awarded in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interiors Version 1.0 Gold Rating The HKMA implemented a number of energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption6 in 2022 was 4,996.4 megawatt-hours (2.8 megawatt-hours per person7), down 24.4% from 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions8 in 2022 were 2,996.4 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per person), down 38.2% from 2015 (Figure 2). Figure 1 Figure 2 Greenhouse Gas Emissions Intensity (Scopes 1 and 2) The HKMA encourages paperless internal operations. In addition, the HKMA has implemented a print management system under which staff must log in to a printer to confirm each print request, helping to reduce unnecessary printing and toner consumption. Where printing is necessary, double-sided and black-and-white printing is encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic record-keeping system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 metric tonnes (0.0114 metric tonnes per person), down 65.3% from 2015 (Figure A). Figure A: Paper Consumption Intensity The HKMA’s waste management efforts continue to follow the “4R” principle. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA also reduces electronic waste through the adoption of technological solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit analysing the composition of waste generated by its offices. The audit found that food waste accounted for a significant proportion of total waste, prompting the HKMA to launch a food waste recycling programme (see “Enhancing Waste Management” on page 41). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022, including general waste and recyclables, was 242.0 metric tonnes (0.135 metric tonnes per person), down 4.8% from 2015 (Figure 3). The fluctuations in the trend were mainly attributable to work-from-home arrangements implemented during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations after the fifth wave of the pandemic. Figure 3 Non-hazardous Waste Intensity The HKMA gives top priority to waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing and recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste from its daily operations, including plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood and electronic products, and to provide recommendations on waste reduction. Based on the audit findings, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, installing food waste collection bins in all pantries. Food waste collected each day is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy for electricity generation. Residues generated during the conversion process can also be made into compost for landscaping and agricultural production. Recycling bins are also conveniently located throughout the offices. The HKMA shared recycling tips with staff and placed greater emphasis on further improving the separation of recyclables at source, as well as precautions for handling recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers and beverage bottles. In addition, we continued to organise activities to raise staff’s environmental awareness, explain waste management policies and encourage staff to make good use of the recycling facilities in the offices. Food waste collected each day is transported to an organic resources recovery centre Recycling Plastic Items The HKMA operates two data centres, one for operations and the other for backup. As they account for a major share of the organisation’s overall energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green designs and a range of energy-saving measures, including in-row air-conditioning systems, light-emitting diode lighting and round-the-clock monitoring of electricity-use efficiency. Following the completion of a consultancy study on the green performance of these data centres in 2022, the HKMA is preparing to implement recommendations for improving overall energy efficiency. Preparations have also begun for obtaining green data centre certification. Recognising the importance of building a sustainability culture, the HKMA regularly launches various programmes and activities to educate and encourage staff to develop sustainability-friendly habits and adopt green and digital ways of working. The HKMA shares green living tips and annual office-wide energy and paper consumption statistics with staff, reminding them to help address environmental issues at the individual level. Staff are also encouraged to make suggestions on sustainability matters. Led by a Senior Manager in the Administration Division, a focus group brings together staff from different departments to brainstorm ideas and concrete measures for promoting a green working environment. Focus group members also serve as ambassadors when new green initiatives are launched. The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt more environmentally friendly practices and has introduced a number of measures to enhance the operational efficiency of the HKMA, the financial industry and the economy as a whole, while minimising resource consumption. The HKMA’s Submission Through Electronic Transmission system (STET) is a one-stop platform that enables banks to submit documents electronically to the HKMA, covering various regular returns required on a weekly, monthly, quarterly or annual basis. Another system, e-Delivery, is a secure electronic communication channel through which the HKMA issues information such as circulars and guidelines to banks. The two systems help save a substantial amount of paper each year. In handling banking complaints and enforcement work, the HKMA has adopted measures to support paperless document submission, enabling bank customers to lodge complaints through electronic channels and online forms. The HKMA is also developing a next-generation management information system to facilitate complaint handling and the transition from paper to digital records. To reduce paper consumption, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU)9 has adopted digital signatures in its daily communications with participants, including the issuance of circulars, account-opening and account-termination letters, and responses to audit confirmations. Going forward, the CMU will continue to explore further green initiatives, including the adoption of automated electronic processes for internal and external communications. By promoting the use of the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored value facilities, the HKMA encourages the public to make greater use of electronic payment methods in place of cash and physical cheques. More information on the FPS and stored value facilities is provided in the chapter “Hong Kong’s International Financial Centre Status” in the HKMA Annual Report 2022. Sending electronic lai-see is simple and convenient, and reduces the use of physical lai-see envelopes and banknotes, thereby helping promote Hong Kong’s sustainable development. To this end, the HKMA continued its active promotion across various social media and traditional platforms, encouraging the public to send electronic lai-see during the Lunar New Year through online or mobile banking services using the FPS or other e-wallet services. Major banks and e-wallet operators also organised various campaigns to attract users to electronic lai-see, such as offering festive user interfaces, enhanced features for greater convenience, lucky draws and cash rebates. The HKMA promotes electronic lai-see on social media For members of the public who choose to give physical lai-see during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA continues to encourage them to use “good-as-new notes”, namely used notes that remain in excellent condition, for their lai-see packets. Good-as-new notes reduce the need to print new banknotes, thereby reducing environmental impacts. Feedback from the note-issuing banks indicates that public acceptance of good-as-new notes has increased in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts to promote coin recycling.
