Coins collected under the Programme are recirculated to meet public demand, improving the efficiency of coin circulation and reducing the need to mint new coins. The Programme operates two Coin Carts and has so far served more than one million customer visits, collecting over 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HK$1.3 billion. In 2022, around 78% of users chose to use some or all of the value of their coins to top up their stored value facility accounts. The HKMA has maintained its collaboration with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service by deploying Coin Carts to collect coins on flag days held by non-governmental organisations, in support of social services. Coin-counting machines on a Coin Cart Launched in 2014, the Coin Collection Programme is the world’s first systematic coin collection programme to adopt a mobile vehicle concept. Over the years, it has received a number of local and international awards in recognition of its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin handling. The Programme operates two Coin Carts, each equipped with two high-speed coin-counting machines to collect coins exchanged by members of the public. Members of the public may choose to exchange their coins for banknotes, use them to top up stored value facility accounts such as Octopus cards or e-wallets, or donate them to The Community Chest. In addition to collecting coins, the Coin Carts are occasionally deployed for various educational activities, such as student visits.

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency (HKQAA) conducted an independent verification of the climate targets (the “Climate Targets”) of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (the “HKMA”). The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual (the “SBTi Corporate Manual”). The purpose of this verification was to verify whether the Climate Targets had been developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. The verification was conducted in accordance with International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information,” issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to form an opinion and conclusion at a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was determined in accordance with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the information. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this verification, HKQAA provides reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. Siu-yan Shum Head of Audit Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency March 2023 Verification Statement Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency (HKQAA) conducted an independent verification of the 2022 environmental data (the “2022 Data”) of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (the “HKMA”). The 2022 Data includes total energy consumption, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions intensity, paper consumption intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rate for 2022, as well as changes in these data compared with 2015 levels. The HKMA’s greenhouse gas emissions data was prepared in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (the “GHG Protocol”), jointly published by the World Resources Institute (“WRI”) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (“WBCSD”). The scope of verification covered relevant data for the period from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2022, as well as relevant data for the period from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015 used for annual performance comparisons. The scope of verification covered a total of six office and warehouse premises: four offices at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place, and 4) Kowloon Commerce Centre; and two warehouses at 5) Roxy Industrial Centre and 6) Chong Lee Centre, located in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The purpose of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance regarding the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA’s data collection mechanism. Within the scope of verification, HKQAA reviewed selected representative data and supporting evidence from the six premises. The verification was conducted in accordance with International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information,” issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to form an opinion and conclusion at a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was determined in accordance with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tested the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing selected sample data to its sources. It also reviewed the underlying procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation and internal checking, and conducted reliability tests. The verification process also included verifying the internal data collection and management mechanism, interviewing representatives responsible for preparing the 2022 Data, and selecting representative data and information for examination. Relevant source data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the information. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. HKQAA’s verification team was not involved in the preparation of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, HKQAA provides reasonable assurance regarding the 2022 Data and concludes that: • The 2022 Data is materially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA’s overall data collection mechanism is adequate. Siu-yan Shum Head of Audit Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency March 2023

Expanding and accelerating climate action has become the most pressing issue of our time. Nearly half of this critical decade for addressing the climate crisis has already passed. We need to reduce global carbon emissions by more than 40% during this decade to have any hope of limiting global warming to within 1.5 degrees Celsius. Yet greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach record highs. The latest climate science indicates that the window of opportunity to limit the rise in global temperatures to within 1.5 degrees Celsius will soon close. We are already clearly experiencing the impacts of a 1.1-degree Celsius increase in temperature—extreme weather events such as record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding and storms are occurring frequently around the world, with each event more serious than the last. Hong Kong is no exception. Last September, soon after being battered by a powerful super typhoon, we experienced a once-in-a-century rainstorm. Despite our sound infrastructure and ability to respond swiftly to disasters, the impact was still extremely severe, with widespread flooding, transport disruptions and damage to roads in many areas. All these events serve as a clear reminder that decisive and ambitious climate action cannot be delayed. Asia faces particularly significant challenges on the path towards a low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development and sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that strike an appropriate balance between climate action, economic growth and social inclusion. This is by no means easy. Due to the region’s rapid economic development and population growth, it accounts for more than half of global carbon emissions. At the same time, the Asia-Pacific region’s high population density and geographical location also make it vulnerable to rising sea levels and extreme weather. As the region’s economies are at different stages of development, the low-carbon transition will create new opportunities for some economies, but securing the necessary transition finance will pose an enormous challenge for others. Market estimates suggest that the Asia-Pacific region will require more than US$3 trillion in low-carbon transition investment annually over the next 30 years. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong has both the capability and the responsibility to harness the power of finance to support the low-carbon transition across Asia. As a banking regulator, market facilitator and responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has devoted substantial efforts to the sustainability agenda. The chapters of this report describe the various specific measures and initiatives introduced by the HKMA over the past year. In addition, to strengthen the HKMA’s internal governance framework and more effectively co-ordinate sustainability work across different functions, we established the Green and Sustainability Steering Committee last year. For details of the Steering Committee, please refer to the new chapter entitled “Sustainability Governance”. Hong Kong banks play an important role in supporting Asia’s transition to net zero. In addition to performing our traditional role as a banking regulator by ensuring through our day-to-day supervisory work that banks properly manage climate risks, we also act as a facilitator, supporting the banking sector in financing the low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green classification framework to help banks and other financial institutions identify environmentally sustainable activities, thereby enabling them to align their business decisions with global climate goals. We launched a prototype green classification framework for consultation in May and are now refining the framework based on feedback received during the consultation. Furthermore, as demand grows for higher-quality and more globally comparable sustainability disclosures, the HKMA is working with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board in June—a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator is not limited to developing frameworks and rules; we are also committed to addressing the industry’s pain points. Many banks currently face data constraints that make it difficult to conduct physical risk assessments. In view of this, the HKMA will soon launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform. By simply entering a property address, banks will be able to assess the impact of physical hazards on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios, helping them manage the relevant climate risks. As a major international financial centre and sustainable finance hub in Asia, Hong Kong has long served as a bridge, directing international investment towards sustainable development projects in Asia and supporting the region’s low-carbon transition. In recent years, international green and sustainable bonds arranged in Hong Kong have accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, clearly outpacing other jurisdictions. Of particular note, the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong in 2023 for the third and second consecutive years respectively, once again affirming Hong Kong’s important role as a green gateway connecting the Mainland with the rest of the world. The flourishing of Hong Kong’s sustainable bond market is partly attributable to the demonstration effect of the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing approximately US$25 billion worth of green bonds to institutional and retail investors. We have seized every issuance opportunity to continuously innovate and expand the features of green bonds, including their currencies, tenors and distribution channels, laying the groundwork for other public- and private-sector green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bond in 2022, we issued the world’s first tokenised government green bond in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the second issuance of tokenised green bonds. Denominated in four major currencies and issued in digitally native form, these were the world’s first multi-currency digital green bonds. At the same time, we have proactively introduced various measures to enhance the vitality and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem. These efforts cover a range of areas, including skills training, data enhancement, green fintech and transition finance. In talent development in particular, we introduced a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners in 2023, providing banking practitioners with a structured curriculum to deepen their understanding and professional knowledge of green and sustainable finance. Transition finance is another key area of our work. It provides funding for decarbonisation activities in high-emitting and hard-to-abate sectors, preventing these sectors from being unable to transition due to a lack of financial support. To support the sound development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand Hong Kong’s green classification framework to cover transition activities. We will also broaden the scope of the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme, which provides subsidies to eligible bond issuers and borrowers, to include transition bonds and loans, thereby encouraging companies in the region to raise transition finance in Hong Kong. In addition, we will strengthen engagement with relevant stakeholders and attract private-sector investment in sustainable development projects that have traditionally faced difficulty securing financing through public-private partnerships and blended finance. Some of the above work requires cross-sector collaboration and is co-ordinated mainly by the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional collaboration is equally important. In addition to our long-standing collaboration with the International Finance Corporation on the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office became a founding member of the Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership in 2023. The Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero also announced plans to establish a chapter in Hong Kong. Through these partnerships, we hope to promote skills training and knowledge sharing, thereby supporting the channelling of capital towards sustainable development projects in the region and around the world. To foster new business development and knowledge exchange, the HKMA also helped organise the inaugural Hong Kong Green Week earlier this year, attracting more than 1,600 participants from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including leading decision-makers from the global business and financial sectors, to discuss ways to scale up climate finance in the region and forge new partnerships in this area. Chief Executive Mr Eddie Yue delivers remarks at the Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum, the flagship event of Hong Kong Green Week. As manager of Hong Kong’s official reserves and a major global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of green and sustainable asset investment and has progressively expanded the Exchange Fund’s ESG and green asset portfolios across public and private markets. In support of the goal of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s Investment Portfolio by 2050 or earlier, the HKMA added an actively managed global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition last year, while extending the application of a customised low-carbon equity index to another public-market asset portfolio. In addition, the green, social and sustainability bonds prioritised by the HKMA have outperformed their investment benchmarks, demonstrating the proposition of “doing well by doing good”. In private markets, we continued to pursue green-related investment opportunities and became an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. At the end of 2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had fallen by 6% and 46% compared with the 2021 and 2017 levels respectively, and remained below the overall market level. As a sustainable organisation, the HKMA will continue to strive for improvement by setting our sustainability goals and plans around the three pillars of the environment, our employees and social responsibility. Specifically, on our low-carbon transition journey, the HKMA continues to strengthen its capability to address climate change by assessing our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures cover emissions reduction, energy efficiency enhancement and waste management, with the ultimate goal of fulfilling our commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We have formulated plans to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely in the near term and are making good progress towards our interim target for reducing Scope 2 emissions by 2030. To attract and retain outstanding talent to carry out the HKMA’s important functions, the HKMA is committed not only to its green goals but also to promoting the physical and mental well-being of its staff. In addition, by collaborating with various stakeholders, we contribute to building a caring society by promoting financial inclusion, enhancing the public’s financial literacy and raising public awareness of financial fraud prevention. The climate challenge is immense and exceptionally urgent. Economies around the world are moving towards a more sustainable future, a process that is expected to bring enormous changes to financing activities and asset allocation. This transformation entails considerable risks, but it will also bring unprecedented opportunities. As a major global sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has a responsibility to take the lead in addressing these challenges. At the same time, we are well positioned to build on this momentum. The HKMA will fully support the industry in financing the low-carbon transition; continue to lead by example as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation; and work with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

Climate change risks and other sustainability issues are global in nature. The HKMA’s objective in its sustainability work is to lead by example through its own policies and operations, ensure that Hong Kong’s financial system and the HKMA itself are resilient to climate change risks, and support the transition to more sustainable economic development. Through active participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also contribute to the formulation of green and sustainable finance policies and standards at the regional and global levels. As the banking regulator, the HKMA will further strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. Specifically, key priorities include: conducting a new round of thematic reviews of banks’ climate risk management practices and a new round of consultation meetings as part of the assessment of banks’ progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management; continuing the work of incorporating climate considerations into the HKMA’s supervisory review process; completing the second round of the industry-wide climate risk stress test, providing guidance to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing observations and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures, including working with relevant local authorities to align the applicable requirements with the International Financial Reporting Standards Sustainability Disclosure Standards as the global baseline, and preparing for the implementation of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s Pillar 3¹ framework for climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidance on best practices in transition planning with the industry. To foster the sound development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will continue to keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments and maintain communication with the industry to ensure that banks adopt appropriate sales processes. In addition, the HKMA will act as a facilitator to promote the development of the green finance ecosystem and support banks in financing the economic transition. We will soon publish a local green taxonomy and continue to broaden its coverage to encompass more activities, including transition activities. Meanwhile, we will continue to explore the use of technology solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures; one example is the forthcoming cloud-based platform designed to facilitate banks’ physical risk assessments. To enhance practitioners’ professional capabilities, we will also develop the Professional Level module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners in 2024. Hong Kong is well positioned to serve as a regional and international sustainable finance hub. To fulfil this role, the HKMA is assisting the Government in implementing the proposal in the 2023–24 Budget to expand the scope of the Government Green Bond Programme to cover sustainable finance projects, thereby deepening the development of the local green and sustainable bond market; at the same time, through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme, we will attract more green financing activities, including transition finance activities, to Hong Kong. We will also continue to encourage more governments, institutions and corporates to raise green funds through Hong Kong and explore potential synergies between green finance and technology. In addition, we will continue to assist in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. As Co-Chair of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), we will continue to work closely with other agencies and government bureaux and departments to coordinate cross-sectoral policies and initiatives that promote the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In 2024, the Steering Group will focus on three areas: sustainability disclosures, the application of technology, and transition finance. As another key priority, through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will continue to jointly launch various targeted programmes across Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing distinctive market insights and targeted professional training for banks, and offering practical guidance to help banks support financial institutions in developing their own differentiated green transition pathways. In 2024, we will also strive to deepen our collaboration with the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, the Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment, and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has committed the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments through a three-pronged responsible investment approach, ensuring portfolio resilience throughout the journey towards net zero. Recognising that the goals of the Paris Agreement can only be achieved through an economy-wide transition, we are refining our net-zero strategy to focus, subject to the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives, on assets that can deliver positive climate benefits to the real economy. As an environmentally responsible organisation, the HKMA’s decarbonisation strategy will continue to evolve to reflect the latest market, regulatory, technological and other climate-related developments. To further strengthen the HKMA’s climate resilience and risk preparedness, we will explore the feasibility of using technology solutions to assess the impact of physical risks on our offices. In addition, we will continue to actively encourage staff participation in our sustainability efforts, including launching campaigns to foster sustainable habits and enhancing office processes and practices. The HKMA will also continue to maintain a consistent, efficient and sustainable procurement approach, including assessing suppliers’ ESG practices when selecting suppliers and renewing contracts. Building on the green data centre certification obtained in 2023, the HKMA is committed to upholding the prescribed certification standards. For regular upgrades to data centre facilities, we will incorporate green designs and practices in addition to keeping abreast of the latest technological developments. Meanwhile, we will continue to reduce electronic waste through the application of technology and convergence, and actively modernise internal systems to improve efficiency and minimise potential risks as far as possible. Finally, in relation to our social focus, the HKMA will identify more community service opportunities for colleagues and work with the industry to promote financial inclusion, improve financial literacy, and raise public awareness of precautions against financial fraud.

Climate change affects every aspect of human life, and everyone can contribute to mitigating its impacts. Through its multiple roles as a central banking institution, banking regulator, market facilitator, responsible investor and sustainable organisation, the HKMA contributes to promoting and accelerating the transition to net zero emissions in Hong Kong and across Asia. The HKMA has established a robust sustainability governance framework to lead the formulation of its relevant strategies and policies; oversee the implementation of related initiatives; and ensure that sustainability considerations are integrated into the HKMA’s own operations and working practices. As part of its commitment to sound corporate governance, the HKMA has established a robust sustainability governance framework for its sustainability-related work, with clear accountability arrangements and a high degree of transparency. This governance framework ensures that sustainability considerations are effectively integrated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, and provides effective mechanisms for monitoring and evaluating the progress and effectiveness of its sustainability work. The HKMA’s sustainability governance framework comprises: the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant sub-committees, which monitor and advise on the HKMA’s work, including its sustainability work; the Green and Sustainability Steering Committee (Steering Committee), chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, which provides management-level leadership for the HKMA’s overall environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategies and policies; in the area of responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, which coordinates and oversees ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office; and, in other functional areas, relevant committees and working groups, which plan and implement related sustainability initiatives covering banking and market development as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (CASG), co-initiated by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the work of financial regulators, government bureaux and departments, industry stakeholders and other stakeholders to accelerate the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In view of the significant expansion in the scope of the HKMA’s sustainability work over the past few years, we established the Steering Committee in October as a new central platform to lead and more effectively coordinate all sustainability work across the HKMA’s different functional areas1. It provides guidance on the formulation of strategies, policies and plans concerning ESG-related matters in the four functional areas of banking, market development, Exchange Fund investment and internal operations; oversees the implementation of ESG-related plans by the HKMA’s functional departments; assesses the HKMA’s performance and effectiveness in achieving its ESG objectives; and oversees external communication strategies. The Steering Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with the three Deputy Chief Executives serving as standing members. We also invite Executive Directors responsible for key functions related to green and sustainability matters to attend Steering Committee meetings and report on the key outcomes of their work and future plans. The Steering Committee meets regularly and is supported by relevant working groups under the HKMA’s banking departments, Corporate Development and Services Division, External Department and Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition to formulating and implementing its own sustainability initiatives, the HKMA and the SFC jointly initiated the establishment of the CASG2 in May 2020. As a cross-agency platform, the CASG provides strategic direction and coordinates cross-sectoral efforts by the financial sector to address climate and environmental risks, with a view to reinforcing Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance centre in Asia and globally. For details of the CASG’s work, see the chapter “Strengthening the Green and Sustainable Finance Ecosystem”.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are affected by various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA is committed to formulating various policy measures to strengthen the banking system’s resilience to climate risks. In August, the HKMA issued a circular on net-zero transition planning, setting out high-level principles to assist banks in maintaining safety and soundness during the economy’s transition to net-zero emissions. Following the issuance of the circular, we conducted a survey of selected banks in the fourth quarter to understand their transition planning practices. Based on the survey findings, we will share observations and best practices on transition planning with the industry and organise seminars or workshops to facilitate the exchange of experience within the industry. Regarding disclosure requirements, in light of the latest international developments, including the publication of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards in June and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s consultation in November on a Pillar 3 disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks, the HKMA is intensifying its work to enhance the sustainability-related disclosure framework for Hong Kong banks. Specifically, the HKMA is working with relevant local authorities and stakeholders to develop a comprehensive roadmap for Hong Kong that aligns with the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. During the year, the HKMA strengthened its supervision of banks’ climate risk management and provided advice to help banks further enhance their climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA made significant progress in implementing its two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process. Climate risk management has now become a standing agenda item at prudential meetings with bank management. Banking supervisors also use an enhanced CAMEL rating system1, which incorporates climate risk factors, to assess banks’ risk profiles and risk management systems. As part of implementing the two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, the HKMA revised the “Greenness” assessment framework to focus on banks’ transition planning practices. The HKMA is also reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks for addressing climate risks. Key work priorities under the two-year plan in 2023 Following the end of the 12-month implementation period for compliance with Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1, “Climate Risk Management”, the HKMA commenced a round of thematic reviews of climate-related risk governance in the second quarter. The thematic reviews covered four key areas: governance structures for climate-related risks, oversight of climate strategies, oversight of climate-related risk management, and institutional culture, awareness and communication. The HKMA made a number of enhancements to its climate risk stress-testing framework, including the introduction of a new five-year scenario to assess the potential impact on banks of concurrent economic and climate-related shocks. Following these enhancements, and as part of the HKMA’s regular programme of supervisor-led stress tests, the second round of climate risk stress tests commenced in June to comprehensively assess banks’ climate risk exposures and further enhance their capacity to manage climate risks. A total of 44 banks participated in this round of stress tests, representing an increase of more than 60% compared with the inaugural pilot exercise in 2021. The HKMA also held a Climate Risk Stress Testing Forum in November, attended by as many as 300 banking practitioners. By facilitating the sharing of experience among banks, the event helped deepen the industry’s overall understanding of climate risk measurement. The HKMA also conducted a series of consultation meetings to review banks’ progress in implementing the HKMA’s Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1, “Climate Risk Management”. The HKMA met with bank management to discuss their work on climate risk management and the common challenges facing the industry, and reviewed information provided by banks and other publicly available information to assess their progress. The HKMA provided banks with targeted advice, encouraging and supporting them to continue strengthening their climate risk management capabilities in line with the HKMA’s supervisory expectations. With growing global attention to climate change and efforts to address it, the HKMA has observed increasing demand for green and sustainable investment products, and some banks are offering related products to meet customer demand. In view of this, the HKMA completed a thematic review of banks’ sale of green and sustainable investment products and issued a circular in November setting out the standards banks are expected to meet and sharing observed good practices. The circular covers various areas, including product due diligence, disclosure, governance and controls, staff training, and bookkeeping and record-keeping, with the aim of mitigating potential greenwashing risks and strengthening investor confidence, thereby promoting the sound development of related investment activities. The HKMA will continue to monitor the latest trends and market developments. The HKMA is committed to promoting the use of technology in green and sustainable banking. For example, technology can improve data availability and risk analysis, thereby strengthening banks’ capacity to manage climate risks. The HKMA will soon launch a pilot cloud-based platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on residential and commercial buildings under different climate scenarios. In addition, the HKMA continues to collaborate with other central banks and regulators to explore how technological solutions can facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also encourages the adoption of sustainable approaches to combating money laundering through the application of advanced analytics and artificial intelligence, thereby reducing the consumption of compliance-related resources. In 2023, the HKMA launched an online common data submission platform to fully automate the financial crime risk data collection process, thereby enhancing banks’ operational processes for the sustainable submission of anti-money laundering-related data. In September, the HKMA organised the “Green Fintech Competition” to identify market-ready solutions that could help the banking industry address challenges relating to: (i) net-zero transition or transition planning; (ii) climate risk management; (iii) green and sustainable finance; and (iv) sustainability- or climate-related disclosures and reporting. The competition attracted more than 85 submissions from around 70 companies. In December, the HKMA organised the “Green and Sustainable Banking Conference”, providing a platform for the banking and technology sectors to explore the role of low-carbon technology and green fintech in the net-zero transition of Hong Kong and the Mainland, while also announcing the results of the “Green Fintech Competition”. The event attracted around 400 participants from banks, technology companies, regulatory authorities and academia. To enhance transparency across financial markets and improve consistency in green and sustainable finance decision-making, the HKMA developed a local green taxonomy framework with the assistance of a consultancy. In May, the HKMA published a discussion paper on the “Prototype of a Green Classification Framework for Hong Kong” to solicit stakeholders’ views on the establishment and implementation of a green taxonomy. Based on the consultation results, the HKMA is refining the prototype framework and identifying additional areas for the next stage of framework development. The HKMA participates in the work of the Financial Action Task Force, which has identified environmental crime as a predicate offence for money laundering. In view of the interconnectedness between anti-money laundering and environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues, this area is attracting increasing attention from regulators. Recognising the potential risks that climate change may pose to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its ongoing surveillance work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. As a member of the Financial Stability Board’s working group on transition planning, the HKMA participates in analysing the interactions between the transition plans of financial and non-financial companies and financial stability, enabling policymakers to develop a forward-looking and dynamic perspective for examining climate-related financial risks. In terms of research, the HKMA conducts various applied research projects exploring the impact of climate change and broader ESG issues on the financial sector and the economy. Research topics include the climate risk exposures of the banking sector and investment funds2, ESG fund flows3, the impact of climate change on property prices4, and the ripple effects of corporate ESG performance throughout global supply chains5. The findings of these studies enhance the HKMA’s understanding of the implications of climate change and ESG issues for financial stability and facilitate the formulation of relevant policies. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA also shares its research findings with a broad range of stakeholders through international events on climate-related issues, the HKMA Research Memorandum series and other channels. The HKMA’s “Liquidity Facilities Framework” is a secured standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. In line with the NGFS’s recommendations, the HKMA has incorporated sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under the framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps facilitate international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, while drawing insights from these discussions to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA is committed to enhancing market awareness and participation, providing the necessary infrastructure and enablers, supporting international initiatives, and aligning with global standards. During the year, the HKMA worked closely with local and international partners to build a more vibrant ecosystem and further advance green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategies. The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced key initiatives to support Hong Kong in capturing sustainable finance opportunities, with major areas of work covering sustainability disclosures, ecosystem enhancement, transition finance, and green fintech. Specifically, a Sustainability Disclosures Working Group was established to develop a roadmap for Hong Kong’s adoption of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. The roadmap will cover four key areas: sustainability reporting, assurance, data and technology, and skills training. A Transition Finance Working Group was also established to explore ways to support financial institutions and corporates in transition planning and reporting. The Steering Group also strengthened the sustainable finance ecosystem through cross-sector capacity building and data enhancement. On data in particular, we continued to promote the use of the climate and environmental risk questionnaire for non-listed companies2, launched by the Steering Group in collaboration with CDP in 2022. The Steering Group will continue to keep abreast of the latest developments in green and sustainable finance and enhance Hong Kong’s position as a regional and global green and sustainable finance hub. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced three new key initiatives to capture the financing and investment opportunities arising from the Asia-Pacific region’s low-carbon transition. To support capacity building in the industry, the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance under the Steering Group implemented the Government’s Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme, which provides subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates undertaking green and sustainable finance-related training and acquiring relevant qualifications. As of December 2023, a total of 46 international and local training programmes or qualifications had been registered as eligible programmes or qualifications under the scheme, and more than 560 subsidy applications had been approved. The HKMA also launched the foundation level of a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners. The module aims to foster talent development in the banking sector and enhance practitioners’ overall professional competence. In 2024, the HKMA will continue to work with the banking industry to develop the professional level of the module to meet the industry’s rapidly growing demand for green and sustainable finance professionals. To help financial institutions and corporates, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, better understand key climate- and sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management, sustainability reporting, greenhouse gas emissions calculation and transition planning, the HKMA collaborated during the year with relevant government bureaux and departments as well as global partners such as CDP, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ)3 and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF)4 to organise a series of seminars and thematic workshops, attracting participants from the financial services and corporate sectors. For students, following the launch of the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative in 2022, training programmes were held in January and February 2023 to deepen interns’ and university bachelor’s degree graduates’ understanding of sustainable finance. Recognising the potential of technology to bridge climate-related data gaps and improve data quality, the HKMA is committed to making relevant data more readily accessible and usable, and enhancing data quality to support informed decision-making and effective climate action. In February 2024, the Steering Group launched a series of website enhancements to provide financial institutions, corporates and the public with a one-stop source of information on green and sustainable finance. Key enhancements included an electronic sustainability disclosure platform, greenhouse gas emissions calculation and estimation tools, and more centralised, user-friendly and searchable data and resources. During Hong Kong Green Week, the Steering Group also co-organised the “Climate Business Forum: Asia Pacific” technology event with Cyberport and Invest Hong Kong to showcase leading green innovation solutions and Hong Kong’s strengths in green technology. “Hong Kong Green Week – Finance Stream” was held from 26 February to 1 March 2024, during which sustainability-themed events attracted more than 1,600 guests from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including representatives from financial institutions, corporates, central banks, international organisations, government agencies, academia and consulting firms. The flagship event of Hong Kong Green Week was the “Climate Business Forum: Asia Pacific”, co-hosted by the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation. The forum brought together more than 400 guests, including top decision-makers in global business and finance, to discuss solutions for unlocking climate finance in the Asia-Pacific region. The two-day event explored a broad range of topics, including energy transition, decarbonisation of heavy industries, the circular economy, the future development of sustainable finance, and emerging climate technologies in emerging and developing markets in the Asia-Pacific region. The forum received support from public- and private-sector organisations, which co-organised more than 10 roundtables, seminars and other networking events. Topics covered climate finance, carbon markets, electric vehicle supply chains, financing for the net-zero transition, green taxonomies, and financing for green development in Belt and Road regions. In addition, the HKMA and the International Monetary Fund co-hosted the “Asia Climate Finance Roundtable” on 29 February 2024 to explore key measures for scaling up climate finance and the role of central banks and regulators in climate risk management. These events formed part of the HKMA’s overall efforts to foster and enrich Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance ecosystem, serving as useful platforms for participants to promote new business development, share knowledge, and explore new opportunities to address climate financing challenges in the Asia-Pacific region. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks5 as a collaborative platform bringing together financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop green commercial banking. Since March 2021, the Alliance has held 22 training events and roundtables, attracting more than 7,300 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In October, the Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB published their second thought leadership report, entitled “Developing an Ambitious Climate Strategy for Green Banking: A Case Study”. In October, the Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB jointly published the thought leadership report “Developing an Ambitious Climate Strategy for Green Banking: A Case Study”. During the year, the HKMA Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office joined the newly established Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment (CASI) and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership (GIFP) initiated by the Belt and Road Initiative International Green Development Coalition. Collaboration with CASI and GIFP will facilitate capacity building and knowledge sharing, and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects in Asia and beyond. In August 2023, GFANZ announced the establishment of its Hong Kong Chapter to support the net-zero efforts of financial institutions in Hong Kong and Mainland China. The HKMA supports GFANZ’s work in an advisory capacity. To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance, and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018. The HKMA assists with green bond issuances under the programme. To date, the Government has issued approximately US$25 billion equivalent in institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 70 green government projects, such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance the programme’s transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. The Government continued its regular institutional green bond issuances in the 2023–24 financial year and issued approximately US$6 billion equivalent in green bonds in June. The triple-currency offering covered bonds of various tenors denominated in US dollars, euros and renminbi, attracting different types of investors and receiving an enthusiastic response, with subscriptions totalling nearly US$30 billion equivalent. The issuance size of the renminbi bonds increased from RMB10 billion in January to RMB15 billion, and a 10-year renminbi bond was introduced for the first time, helping to extend the Government’s renminbi yield curve and further enrich the range of offshore renminbi products. The enthusiastic response from global investors to the Government’s green bond issuances reflected investors’ recognition of Hong Kong’s commitment to promoting green and sustainable development. In October, the Government issued the second batch of green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion, further promoting market development and financial inclusion. The issuance provided the public with an investment opportunity offering stable returns, enabling them both to participate in and benefit from the development of green finance in Hong Kong.

As a major global asset owner and manager, the HKMA plays a pivotal role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate agenda. The HKMA has long been a pioneer in responsible investment. Since 2015, the HKMA has been leading investment in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to exercise active ownership and integrate environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth”1, the HKMA believes that due consideration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors helps mitigate relevant investment risks while unlocking the long-term sustainable value of investments. As one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and set a “net-zero emissions by 2050” target2 for its “portfolio”, the HKMA is committed to continuously advancing its responsible investment journey, with an emphasis on sustainability, particularly the urgent issue of climate change, with a view to enhancing the resilience of the Exchange Fund and achieving better risk-adjusted long-term returns. As a responsible investor, the HKMA contributes to building a robust green and sustainable finance ecosystem by partnering with like-minded investors, regulators and international organisations to develop industry operating standards and promote the adoption of responsible investment across the financial industry and central banking community. Through stewardship and collaborative initiatives, the HKMA strives to foster a future in which finance and sustainable development advance in tandem. Figure 1 The Exchange Fund’s responsible investment journey Comprehensive and reliable ESG information is essential for integrating sustainability and planning a credible climate transition to achieve net-zero targets. To fulfil its commitments to support the Glasgow Declaration3 of the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the strategic plan of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, the HKMA leads by example by preparing this chapter on the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The overarching guiding principle sets the tone for the HKMA to pursue responsible investment while taking into account the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors their implementation through regular meeting reports from the Sustainable Investment Team of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 2, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Strategy Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s ESG initiatives. Proposals and work progress discussed at the ESG Committee’s quarterly meetings are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition, the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and attended by the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, meets semi-annually to provide guidance on ESG policies and initiatives across the HKMA’s different functions, including the Exchange Fund Investment Office, in pursuit of the HKMA’s overall ESG objectives. Figure 2 Responsible investment governance structure of the Exchange Fund Investment Office As shown in Figure 1, the Exchange Fund Investment Office embarked on its responsible investment journey in 2016, initially focusing on managing ESG risks that could affect the Exchange Fund’s financial performance. As sustainability evolved rapidly and moved beyond risk considerations to become a strategic priority for leading institutions worldwide, the Exchange Fund Investment Office revisited its approach to responsible investment. July 2023 marked another milestone, when the Exchange Fund Investment Office established a new Business Strategy Division led by the Chief Strategy Officer to coordinate and lead its strategic development, incorporating the responsible investment task force formerly under the Risk Management and Compliance Division—now known as the Sustainable Investment Team. This strategic realignment reflects the HKMA’s shift in responsible investment focus from a risk-based approach to a more proactive and forward-looking stance in addressing investment-related sustainability matters. The Sustainable Investment Team works closely with different teams across the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists its senior management in managing ESG risks and opportunities, particularly those related to climate, across various investment portfolios: Public market investments—The Credit, Rules and Compliance Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, reviews the integration of ESG factors into the credit risk model with input from the Sustainable Investment Team, and monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Sustainable Investment Team participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Promoting Active Ownership” under “Risk Management” on page 40 for details). Private market investments—The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal conducted by the private market investment and risk management teams. The HKMA recognises that the physical and transition risks4 arising from climate change, as well as the associated opportunities, may affect the long-term performance and value of the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Emissions Gap Report 20235 published by the United Nations Environment Programme projects that, unless further reductions in greenhouse gas emissions are made worldwide, the global average temperature will rise by 2.5°C to 2.9°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. The urgent need for more ambitious policies, technological development or behavioural changes to contain temperature increases may exacerbate transition risks, such as asset devaluation or stranded-asset shocks. At the same time, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events also pose additional physical risks to investments. The HKMA believes that investing in a greener future is aligned with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives and therefore places particular emphasis on climate-related factors when integrating ESG considerations. In 2022, the HKMA set a target for the Exchange Fund’s “portfolio” to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, further demonstrating its commitment to the global climate agenda. The HKMA continues to strengthen its three-pronged approach, with a clear focus on decarbonisation and transition. The following sections describe this approach in detail. Figure 3 The HKMA’s three-pronged approach to responsible investment In progressing towards its net-zero target, the HKMA favours active engagement over exclusion or divestment from its investable universe. First, maintaining a diversified and robust portfolio is critical to achieving the Exchange Fund’s primary investment objectives. Directly excluding certain sectors or industries would narrow the investable universe, with potential implications for investment returns and risk. By adopting an inclusive approach, the HKMA can seize opportunities to invest in companies undergoing transition and equipped with superior technologies and sound corporate governance to address evolving global climate trends, including companies in high-emitting industries. Second, addressing climate change requires the transition of core “brown” industries. Simply excluding or divesting from relevant investments does not help resolve the issue of carbon emissions. Instead, by deploying strategic capital and exercising active ownership to support these industries, the HKMA encourages them to transition towards sustainable and low-carbon practices, thereby driving positive change both within the industries themselves and globally. In response to market developments, the HKMA is refining its net-zero investment strategy to pursue transition outcomes that align with the net-zero objectives of both the Exchange Fund and the world through a holistic approach, while adhering to its responsible investment guiding principles. By integrating ESG factors into investment decisions, the HKMA continues to pursue sustainable investments and opportunities to facilitate climate transition and enhance the long-term resilience of the Exchange Fund’s portfolio (Figure 4). The HKMA’s responsible investment maintained strong momentum in 2023. In the public markets, the HKMA launched a new actively managed global equity portfolio with sustainability and climate-transition themes, managed by an external investment manager, and extended the application of a customised low-carbon equity index to another externally managed portfolio. In addition, the green, social and sustainability bonds prioritised by the HKMA outperformed the investment benchmark, demonstrating the concept of “doing well by doing good”. In the private markets, the HKMA actively built a resilient long-term growth portfolio, capturing investment opportunities expected to benefit from long-term economic trends such as climate and energy transition. For example, during the year the HKMA invested in two Asia-focused transition investment funds, reflecting its commitment to addressing Asia’s climate-transition needs. Figure 4 Ongoing initiatives to promote ESG investment The HKMA has invested in a company specialising in producing environmentally friendly thermoplastic materials from unsorted household waste, including organic matter such as food waste, and non-recyclable materials. Unlike conventional chemical recycling systems, which rely on energy-intensive, high-temperature environments to produce plastics, the company has pioneered a low-temperature production method powered entirely by solar arrays. Made entirely from waste, this plastic material can serve as an alternative to petroleum-based resins commonly used in industries such as retail and consumer durables, providing a sustainable and versatile option. It is also compatible with existing standard manufacturing processes and cutting-edge technologies such as 3D printing. The company is a staunch supporter of the circular economy. The diagram below illustrates the positive environmental outcomes generated by its advanced plastics production process: Managed by the International Finance Corporation, the MCPP is an innovative initiative that combines funding from institutional investors with the IFC’s own funds to scale up sustainable financing for private companies in emerging markets. The HKMA committed two tranches of US$1 billion each to the MCPP in 2017 and 2019 respectively, and further collaborated with the IFC in 2021 to create “MCPP One Planet”, a new global climate-related investment platform that is also the world’s first Paris-aligned cross-sectoral emerging-market loan portfolio. Through the MCPP, the HKMA has committed to providing loans to 80 sustainable development projects across 19 sectors, including infrastructure, agriculture, real estate and manufacturing, in 38 developing countries. The IFC has collected data on MCPP loans. According to the IFC’s reports, the HKMA’s loan commitments support emerging markets and developing economies in areas including economic transformation and human capital development. Specifically, the projects financed by the HKMA are expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 5.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, equivalent to the greenhouse gas emissions from an average petrol-powered passenger vehicle travelling 14 billion miles. Figure 5 Projected average annual benefits of the HKMA’s loan commitments to the MCPP since 2020 A green and sustainable finance ecosystem is the cornerstone of future global sustainable development. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities.

The HKMA is committed to becoming a sustainable organisation and adopts a multi-pronged approach to reducing its carbon footprint, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In addition to promoting environmental sustainability, the HKMA also places emphasis on staff well-being and social responsibility, and strives to promote financial inclusion and enhance the public’s financial literacy. As a responsible organisation, the HKMA has set sustainability objectives under the three pillars of the environment, staff and social responsibility. The Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee (Steering Committee)1, established in October and chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is the principal decision-making body for corporate sustainability initiatives. The Steering Committee was formerly the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which was responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating its vision, strategies and policies on corporate sustainability and social responsibility matters. At the departmental level, the Assistant Chief Executive (Corporate Development and Operations) oversees the implementation of sustainability activities and regularly submits progress reports to the Steering Committee. The Green Office Task Force and the Volunteer Services Team support the coordination of corporate sustainability work; the former serves as a platform for exchanging ideas on how to create a green workplace, while the latter aims to foster a culture of participation in volunteer activities. The HKMA has developed a roadmap to guide its transformation. The focus is on implementing decarbonisation strategies in its daily operations, including operating green buildings and data centres, adopting green travel practices, using energy-saving measures, digital tools and more environmentally friendly operating models, reducing waste, and building a culture of sustainability. The HKMA also plans to use carbon insetting tools within its own value chain to reduce emissions and to use carbon offsets for emissions that are difficult to reduce. In addition to the above environmental commitments relating to its daily operations, the HKMA continues to introduce greener operational solutions for the wider community, ranging from channels for banks to submit electronic documents and communicate with the HKMA to electronic payment and coin collection schemes for the general public. To strengthen and sustain its operational capabilities, the HKMA employs a professional workforce, builds a talent pool and places emphasis on staff well-being. In terms of social responsibility, the HKMA encourages staff to participate in volunteer and charitable activities; considers engaging social enterprises in procurement; promotes consumer education on financial services; and works with the banking sector to ensure that all segments of society have equitable access to basic banking services. The remainder of this chapter sets out details of the above strategies. Under the HKMA’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Risk Committee2, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the potential risks and threats faced by the HKMA in its daily operations, including those arising from climate change. The physical impacts of climate change, such as flooding or other damage caused by more extreme weather events, may affect the HKMA’s offices and impede staff travel. To manage physical risks, the HKMA regularly updates its business continuity plans to address extreme weather conditions. The HKMA also regularly conducts evacuation and backup facility activation drills to ensure that staff are always prepared to implement business continuity measures. A range of measures to mitigate potential risks has also been incorporated into office design. Transition risks may affect the HKMA’s energy use, air travel and waste disposal. The HKMA has been monitoring its exposure to transition risks by tracking its greenhouse gas emissions, waste generation, energy consumption and paper consumption. The HKMA’s climate target is to achieve net-zero Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 (air travel) greenhouse gas emissions across all areas of its corporate operations by 2050 or earlier. As near-term emission reduction targets, the HKMA plans to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely by converting all its existing vehicles to electric vehicles; and, using 2015 as the baseline year, to reduce Scope 2 emissions intensity by 63% by 2030 or earlier through various decarbonisation and offsetting strategies. Despite the challenges in determining Scope 3 emissions, the HKMA will adopt a multi-pronged approach, as far as practicable, to minimise Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions, such as those arising from paper consumption, waste generation and air travel. The HKMA’s long-term and near-term emission reduction targets were formulated with reference to the Science Based Targets initiative methodology, which was also validated by the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency. The HKMA has appointed the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency to verify the emissions, energy consumption, paper consumption and waste data6 disclosed in this report. The scope and criteria of the verification are set out in the “Verification Statement” section of this report. In 2023, in addition to publishing the 2022 Annual Report, the HKMA issued its first standalone 2022 Sustainability Report. The HKMA’s efforts to enhance ESG reporting were recognised with an ESG Award in the Public Sector/Not-for-profit Organisations category of the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants’ Best Corporate Governance and ESG Awards 2023. The HKMA was the first financial regulator to receive an award in this category. The judging panel commended the HKMA for achieving good ESG standards, presenting a clear and readable Sustainability Report, and demonstrating its commitment to highly transparent and accountable reporting by appointing an independent organisation to verify its target-setting methodology and the environmental data disclosed in the report. In addition, the HKMA received the highest distinction, the Gold Award in the Non-profit and Charitable Organisations category, in the Hong Kong Management Association’s 2023 Best Annual Reports Awards. The judging panel commended the HKMA’s annual report for clearly presenting comprehensive financial information and making effective use of infographics, demonstrating the HKMA’s determination to enhance financial literacy and promote financial inclusion. In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, its staff and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has awarded the HKMA the “15 Years Plus Caring Organisation” logo for 17 consecutive years since 2006. The HKMA is committed to properly managing the environmental impacts of its operations, and its internal Green Office Guidelines provide staff with guidance on resource use and the generation of office waste. The HKMA has incorporated environmental considerations into the design, operation, repair and maintenance of the offices it owns and leases. When offices are refurbished, existing furniture and fit-out materials are reused wherever possible to reduce waste, with priority given to environmentally friendly construction and decorative materials. The HKMA’s consistent adoption of this approach resulted in Gold certifications under LEED7 and BEAM Plus Interiors8 in 2021 and 2022 respectively for parts of its offices in Two International Finance Centre that had completed refurbishment. Improving energy efficiency through the adoption of new technologies and the effective use of existing technologies remains one of the HKMA’s key areas of focus. In addition to promoting good practices, such as switching off unnecessary lighting in work areas outside office hours to conserve electricity, other energy-saving measures include using light-emitting diode lighting, motion sensors, setting indoor air-conditioning temperatures at appropriate levels, and optimising energy use in information technology network infrastructure. The HKMA’s energy consumption continued to decline, reaching 2.59 megawatt-hours9 per capita in 2023, down 29.7% from the 2015 baseline (Figure 1). Given the nature of the HKMA’s daily operations, its greenhouse gas emissions mainly arise from the consumption of electricity generated from fossil fuels. In 2023, the combined intensity of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from purchased fuel and electricity was 1.48 tCO₂e10 per capita, down 45.2% from 2015 (Figure 2). In addition to standardising equipment, office software and meeting facilities, the HKMA has adopted digital tools and technologies, automated and streamlined workflows, created a digital workplace, and strengthened online collaboration within the organisation.11 Paperless meetings have become the HKMA’s primary mode of conducting meetings. To further reduce paper consumption and improve efficiency, electronic processes are used for most internal administrative matters. In addition, the HKMA encourages staff to embrace green and digital ways of working by replacing paper documents and communications with digital alternatives. Implementation of an electronic recordkeeping system is also under way. These green and digital measures have delivered positive results. The HKMA’s paper consumption intensity in 2023 was 11.55 kilograms per capita, representing a substantial reduction of 64.8% from 2015 (Figure 3). As most international events resumed in-person formats after the COVID-19 pandemic, and given the need to promote the development of Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre, overseas business travel by relevant HKMA staff was unavoidable. To reduce carbon emissions from air travel, the HKMA encourages staff attending overseas events to take direct flights or combine different business trips wherever practicable. At the corporate level, the HKMA reduced its Scope 3 emissions by 126 tCO₂e in 2023 through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel. In addition, the HKMA participated in Gold Standard12-certified carbon offset programmes to offset the remaining carbon emissions from air travel; these programmes involve waste-to-energy projects, solar power generation, and the provision of efficient and cleaner cooking facilities in developing countries. The HKMA will continue to make similar arrangements in 2024. The HKMA’s procurement process takes sustainability and environmental considerations into account. As part of a comprehensive review of the organisation’s procurement policies and procedures, the existing practice of procuring green products has been formalised, in compliance with the environmental specifications in the Government’s Green Procurement List, particularly for the procurement of electrical appliances and office consumables. ESG factors and innovative proposals that help enhance productivity and efficiency have also been incorporated into tender evaluation criteria. At the same time, all suppliers are required to undertake to comply with environmental regulations. In accordance with the “4R” principles of Refuse, Reduce, Reuse and Recycle, the HKMA adopts a three-pronged approach to minimising waste generation and managing waste disposal. In addition, the HKMA conducted two waste audits in 2022 and 2023 to assist in formulating targeted waste management strategies. A breakdown of the non-hazardous waste generated, including general waste sent to landfills and various types of recyclable waste, is provided in the “Performance Summary” section on page 56. In 2023, the HKMA participated directly for the first time in the red packet recycling programme organised by the management company of its office building at the International Finance Centre. Staff handed in approximately 3,000 used but still pristine red packets. These were subsequently passed to an environmental organisation for distribution to the public for use during the following Lunar New Year. As the HKMA’s operational and backup data centres account for a major share of the organisation’s overall energy consumption, both data centres have been upgraded to meet the highest standards set by BEAM Plus for existing data centres and achieve optimal Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE)13. In 2023, the HKMA’s two data centres were awarded Gold and Platinum ratings respectively under the BEAM Plus Existing Data Centres assessment guidelines issued in 2021; the HKMA is the first and only organisation in Hong Kong to receive these ratings. Improving the energy efficiency of the two data centres has long been a key focus of the technical team. To this end, the team incorporated green design into the refurbishment works and adopted energy-efficient best practices to lower PUE and achieve the relevant targets, including monitoring the data centres’ environmental facilities around the clock and continuously optimising environmental factors such as airflow and temperature settings. As the technical team continued to improve energy use in the data centres, the HKMA engaged an external consultant in December 2021 to conduct a review comprehensively assessing the data centres’ environmental performance and developing recommendations for further improvement in various areas. The study was completed in mid-2022. Shortly after its completion, the HKMA also began preparations to obtain Green Data Centre certification under the BEAM Plus certification scheme. The certification process was highly comprehensive and rigorous.
